speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RAIL CONNECTION TO BORDER BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like
Inquiries of the Ministry to deal with a question asked on September 9 by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), who is not in his seat this morning. On that occasion he quoted a press dispatch to the effect that the United States Department of State had told the Canadian government that it wanted to start discussions this month on proposals to build a railroad through Canada to Alaska. The hon. member for Peel asked for an indication as to how far these discussions had gone.
Upon looking into the matter I find that a representative of the United States embassy has told the Department of External Affairs that United States officials may wish to have discussions with Canadian officials some time this month on this matter. The question of holding detailed discussions looking to a location survey has been the subject of conversations with the United States embassy, but no decision has as yet been reached as to how far the matter should be gone into at this time. There is little more I can say on that aspect of the question until further information is received from Washington.
It will be recalled that on November 18 last I informed the house, in answer to a question, that the Canadian authorities had been surveying the possibilities of extending the railway from British Columbia to Alaska and were impressed by the high costs of such a project in relation to the expected volume of civilian and military traffic in the near future.
There is no indication that the views of the United States authorities will differ substantially from our present views as to the merits of proceeding with this project at this time. It would seem probable in any case that the demands of the expanding defence programs of both countries, which are making it necessary to reduce expenditures that are not essential to the defence effort, would make it very difficult to find in the near future funds for a sizable project of this kind. I say this because I believe that a number of people in western Canada have the impression that the United States authorities would be prepared to proceed with a location survey and construction of a railway largely, if not entirely, at United States expense.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CLOSING OF SALMON FISHING ON THE FRASER RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries. In view of the fact that the non-arrival of the famous Adams river run of sockeye salmon on the Fraser river is causing great financial loss to the gill-netters on that river, can the parliamentary assistant add anything further to the report given by the Minister of Fisheries the other day?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MacNaughl (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CLOSING OF SALMON FISHING ON THE FRASER RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for having given notice of his question. The


only information I can give him is that contained in the report of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, issued yesterday in Vancouver.
In that report they state that seven days have elapsed since the special closure of sockeye fishing in the Fraser area was announced on September 5. During this period the commission has had widespread observations carried out to determine any new development or condition hearing on the large Adams river sockeye run which failed to appear as it has done on every fourth year for the past twenty years. These observations have failed to reveal the entry of any new supplies of sockeye to inside waters adjacent to the Fraser river mouth. They have also failed to indicate that the quantities of sockeye remaining in the gulf waters are appreciably greater than was estimated a week ago. During the past few days many jumpers from this body of fish could toe seen directly at the mouth of the river and along the flats as the time approached for them to make their upstream migration. During the past seven days the number of sockeye passing upstream toward the spawning grounds has continued to be negligible. The commission will issue another statement in a week's time, on September 19.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, September 12, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at eleven o'clock last evening I was arguing that the minister's budget speech was open to attack by reason of the fact that it indicates a financial policy identical with the policy pursued by the Liberal government throughout world war II. That policy failed to make financially possible in Canada what was physically possible. That policy still is failing to make financially possible in Canada that standard of living and national strength which Canadian resources, material and human, could easily support. That policy during world war II added at least $12,000 million to our national debt. That policy inflated prices, thereby cutting the value of the Canadian dollar more than fifty per cent. That policy indicates a financial system utterly inadequate to the needs of a nation of

rich resources in an age of abundance through the use of machines, modern technological skills and solar power.
I indicated my intention to quote from a speech delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to show that Canada is at present able to take her wartime responsibilities in her stride and at the same time provide her people with a high standard of living. At page 446 of Hansard of the present session we read these words:
We must at the same time maintain a decent standard of living consistent with the requirements of defence. We must show the world that the free democracies can be both prosperous and strong.
And again:
We have never had a larger supply of goods and services and a greater capacity to produce more of these goods and services.
Then on page 447:
First, our industrial capacity is so substantial that we can turn out a considerably larger volume of military equipment and munitions than could possibly be used by our own armed forces.
And again:
Secondly, our own preparedness program, large as . it is in relation to past peacetime performances, will still involve over the next year or eighteen months- barring a major emergency-only a small proportion of Canadian capacity and output, perhaps of the order of six to seven per cent of our gross national product. Requirements coming from abroad, even if they are substantially larger than now indicated, are still likely to be in this period only a small proportion of Canadian industrial production. Our preparedness efforts, including foreign demand, in this period are, therefore, likely to be of the order of less than ten per cent of our gross national product. This is a considerably smaller proportion than what we did during the last war. In 1943 and 1944, the years of our maximum efforts, about forty-two per cent of gross national product was either directly or indirectly related to the pursuit of war.
And again on that same page:
There is substantially increased Canadian ability to produce better and more intricate goods both for peace and war.
And again:
All this is evidence of increased production already achieved, and further expansion in sight is indicative of the fact that Canada has the capacity to take increased preparedness efforts in her stride, and still leave substantial resources free for civilian use.
And on page 448:
But with individuals and governments co-operating there is no reason whatsoever why Canadians should not maintain a high standard of living, and at the same time be adequately prepared to defend their way of life against aggression.
I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce knew what he was talking about. He certainly has his finger on the pulse of Canadian industrial life. Inasmuch as those remarks were made by the minister I contend that certain of the various measures which are being taken in Canada under the budget,
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore and the various things Which are being permitted to occur in Canada, are simply not justified. The people of Canada are entitled to have a high standard of living, but at least eighty per cent of the people are decidedly not getting this.
Let us examine with some care the whole question of production. Looking at the details with which we are all familiar, let us consider this question of production. Does any hon. member in this house believe that we cannot produce all the potatoes that Canada could possibly use, war or no war? Does anyone believe that the people of Canada cannot produce all the vegetables of every kind, war or no war, that the whole people could possibly use, together with enough to support our armed forces? Is there anyone who will say that we cannot produce in Canada all the apples that anybody could use? Let us just stop and look at the prices being asked for apples today in Ottawa and in other towns in Canada. Will anyone say that people in the lower income brackets have access to sufficient apples? Should such a condition be permitted to exist in a nation of plenty like Canada? Under ordinary circumstances is there any question of Canada's ability to produce all the peaches, pears, prunes, cherries and other northern fruits that the people of Canada could possibly use?
Let us now turn to dairy products. As I pointed out the other day, there are few countries in the world better adapted for the production of dairy products than Canada. If we could have even common-sense management in respect of our dairy industry we ought to be able to produce an abundance of every kind of dairy product of which Canadians are capable of producing or using. To say that we have to limit the consumption of dairy products in Canada by any means in order to fight a war is simply to admit that one is out of touch with the facts. Is there any doubt that we could produce all the poultry products that we need in Canada? Surely no one will argue that we cannot.
Then a word with regard to beef. As I pointed out the other day, beef prices are far too high, but it is not beyond the capacity of the Canadian people to produce all the beef that the Canadian people could buy at moderate prices. If prospective producers were guaranteed against loss, they would go into beef production more extensively. Other devices could be used to bring about all the production of beef that we needed in Canada and all that the United States might care to take. Pork is in the same position. Will anyone argue that we cannot produce enough of these products? Will anyone argue that we need, to go on an austerity program with respect to these commodities?

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
Let us turn to grain. We are producing grains fairly abundantly, but I do not think we are producing more than half of what we could prbduce if we really got down to good management of our grain producing capacity in Canada. We are allowing things more or less to drift along. People are mining the soil and are not replenishing the soil with fertilizers. If we really settled down to a policy comparable with the policies adopted by a number of European countries, where they have fewer resources to waste, we should be able to produce grains in much greater abundance than we now seem able to do.
I would suggest that low-cost beef production loans be made available, and that fertilizers be made available at low or no cost. We should fertilize not only our farms but our pastures and hay meadows. If we were to use the best system of crop rotation that can be devised in Canada it would greatly help. If we were to increase beet sugar production in Canada we would increase the fertility of the land wherever the beet sugar industry was carried on and thereby greatly increase the grain we could produce. If we took care of the appropriate mechanization of our farms so that those engaged in farming could get machines at a low rate instead of the exorbitantly high rate which they now have to pay, and about which complaints have been made by hon. members; if we were to make the best possible use of our irrigation facilities, we would get far more production of all kinds of grain and forage crops than we now are getting. If we were to guarantee prices suitably we could get a great quantity of grain produced that is not being produced now. As all hon. members know, grain is the factor that largely determines the amount of production of which we are capable with respect to beef, pork, dairy products, poultry and the like. Consequently our grain production is a matter of vital importance and should be attacked with scientific, purposeful and effective skill.
Is there anyone who will doubt that we can produce all the honey we need, all the sugar that we can consume, or all the coal that we can consume? When we consider matters of this sort we begin to look with some reservation upon certain of the statements being made by members of the government to the effect that we must tighten our belts and go without because we have to fight a war. In fact some of the statements seem to become genuinely extravagant in the light of the actual facts of the Canadian economy.
I should like to give a little more attention to the matter of grain. It now appears that we are going to have a fine crop. I have not had a chance to check in Hansard what the


Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said yesterday, but I gathered that one of the reasons why wide spreads are being permitted between various grades of grain is that he wishes to make our grain attractive to foreign buyers. We do not need1 to worry about foreign buyers. We in Canada can use all the grain we can produce this year. I do not mean that we can eat all the products of all the wheat we can produce, but I argue that if we have the grains on hand during the next few years, which are likely to be years of grave anxiety, we shall be a great deal better off than we shall be if we are too eager to sell the grains which we are now producing in a relatively abundant harvest. I know that is quite contrary to the general theories actuating the people in charge of our grain business; nevertheless I contend there is virtue in what I am saying.
Let me give an illustration. Suppose we begin to store wheat on our farms. There was a time when our fathers used to keep a supply of wheat on their farms for two or three years. Is there any reason why we should not be able to do that? If there is, what is it, and what sense is there in it? People will say: What are you going to do about it? Well, solve the problem. How can you do it? Let us suppose that France would normally buy 100 million bushels of wheat. Of course that is all out of line, so let us cut the figure down to 20 million bushels. If we were to sell that grain to France we would expect United States dollars in return. All we do in effect is take the dollars and distribute them amongst our farmers in payment for the grain. I submit this suggestion with the utmost sincerity, and I challenge anyone to find any fault with it: Is there any conceivable reason why the Bank of Canada could not create the money to pay the farmers for the 20 million bushels of grain? If there is a reason why the Bank of Canada cannot do it, is there any reason why a currency commission, such as we used to operate under in 1915, could not do it? In 1914 and 1915 we had a finance act under which the treasury of Canada could create money. That act was strengthened again in 1923. If the present financial set-up is not as effective as what we had under that legislation, it is high time that we looked into the matter.
If we created money to buy the grain and enabled it to be stored in Canada, we would have the grain. It would belong to the government and would not cost the taxpayers a cent. We would have it right on the farms where we are likely to need it. We would have it right in the communities where, if anything should happen to our transportation system by reason of the exigencies of war, people would not be subjected to the danger

of having to go hungry for want of grain. This is one of the kinds of financial possibility that Social Crediters have in mind when they attack the present financial system. People will say that such action will cause inflation. Of course it will not cause inflation! How would payment for 20 million bushels of wheat with Canadian dollar bills or credit cause any more inflation than the same dollar bills or credit created on the strength of money coming from France?
If we used Bank of Canada credits instead of dollar bills, how could it cause inflation? Let us be realistic in our approach to these matters. If we were a little less anxious to sell our grain abroad and a little more anxious to build up a fine reserve to take care of us over the trying years ahead, I believe we would be walking in the paths of wisdom.
In passing I wish to say that the prices for western wheat are altogether unsatisfactory. I do not wish to be too critical of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I believe he has made a mistake in setting prices with such wide spreads. I do not believe he has given sufficient attention to the fact that the cost of production for the farmer has increased in every single item, even to the extent of a tax deliberately imposed by governments on the gasoline he uses.
It will be argued that we have not the necessary labour to bring about the production which I have envisaged. I imagine that if the truth were known we would find that there are tens of thousands of persons in industry at the present time who are not profitably occupied. Thousands of men, in my opinion, have been taken into the civil service of Canada who are not profitably occupied. In other words, they are not producing their keep. They have been fixed upon the body politic as parasites. The cost of their keep enters into prices, but they are not producing goods, the only source of wealth in Canada. If the government would look at the whole situation with that fact in mind and devise ways and means, I am sure we would find plenty of labour. There are many farmers who are busy only a part of the year. They are necessarily unoccupied for a considerable period of time. If we devise industry such as stock feeding on the farms so that these men can be occupied, we shall have no trouble finding the labour necessary for the increase in production which I have indicated.
I ask this question: Why should anyone in Canada be deprived of those commodities which we can produce in abundance? Why should the prices of those commodities be allowed to be such that people cannot buy
The Budget-Mr. Fulford them? There is no answer to these questions that will stand up to any critical fact-facing mind.
I have not offered any detailed suggestions as to how to deal with the situation technically, but members of the Social Credit movement know how the financial system of Canada can be so managed that all these matters can be taken care of.
I am warning the government that if it neglects this possibility of the most beneficial use of Canada's credit it will do so on its own responsibility, and will be found wanting in the eyes of future generations when men finally become aware of the monstrous outrages that have been perpetrated upon this nation by a faulty and outmoded financial system.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish at the outset to pay particular tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). In this latest budget, which the press of Canada have come to term the baby budget, I feel the minister has adhered to the principles for which the Department of Finance has stood for many years, principles originally outlined by his able predecessor, Mr. Ilsley. We are continuing a pay as you go policy. It is true that there are those who are dissatisfied with the taxes imposed upon certain commodities under this budget, but how can anyone devise a tax that will not pinch somebody? The taxes proposed I think are remarkable in that they pinch so few and upset our economy so little.
Last evening the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), and yesterday afternoon the leader of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), bitterly complained about the tax levied on candy and soft drinks. These commodities are definitely in the luxury class. The people of Canada can well do without too much candy and too many soft drinks. If they can afford to buy those things surely they can afford to pay the not too heavy tax that has been placed upon them. It is not my intention to moralize or tell people what they should or should not eat; but if you ask any pediatrician or any dentist about the effects on the children of Canada of the amount of candy and soft drinks they consume, I think the answer invariably will be that the younger people of this country have been getting altogether too many sweets. For that reason, if for no other, this may be a service in disguise to the younger generation. I realize, of course, that sugar is necessary to produce energy, but on the other hand statistics show

The Budget-Mr. Fulford that we are one of the largest candy eating and soft drink consuming countries in the world.
I do not think enough publicity has been given to the amount we have paid off our national debt since 1946. While Canada has written off approximately $1,500 million from our large public debt, other countries have been adding to theirs. Just this year the President of the United States proposed a budget providing for a deficit of $5 billion, and that was before the Korean trouble was ever thought of. In other words he proposed an addition of $5 billion to the already staggering debt of that country. Canada is indeed the envy of the nations of the world. Taxation here is high; there is no doubt about that. You cannot pay your way and not have high taxation. But compare our taxes with those in effect in Great Britain. All admit that Great Britain has gone through a terrible war ordeal; that she has had to rebuild her cities, and all the rest of it. That is granted. No one would discount for a moment the tremendous contribution in men, resources and money made by Great Britain during two world wars. The fact remains, however, that taxation there has reached such levels that it is becoming detrimental to the initiative of the people. Certainly in Canada our taxation has not reached the point that private enterprise cannot be carried on in an orderly, progressive fashion.
Last evening the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank)-I wish he were in his seat at the moment-suggested that a tax might have been imposed on margarine; and with that suggestion I agree. That would have been a good source of revenue, and at the same time would have helped the dairy farmer by at least making more nearly equal the prices of margarine and butter. However, I definitely refuse to refer to margarine, which is a good wholesome food, as axle grease, as my hon. friend did.
In the Ottawa Journal last evening a Canadian Press dispatch appeared dated Portland, Ontario, September IJl-and incidentally, this matter was also mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. The headline reads, "War widow and six children eke out living from $31 monthly". This case is well known to me, as it happens to be in the riding of Leeds, and I believe a few corrections in the newspaper story are in order. It was not my intention to bring up this matter on the floor of the house, but since it appeared in a Canadian Press dispatch to the Ottawa Journal, and also as a feature article in last evening's Toronto Telegram, complete with pictures, I feel that an explanation is due.


Mr. and Mrs. William Oprey were the parents of three children when, in January of 1949, they were presented with triplets. Immediately following this unique presentation the Department of Veterans Affairs sent an investigator to Portland, and as a result an application was made to the provincial command of the army benevolent fund, following which the accounts having to do with the birth of these triplets were paid in full. I personally interested myself to the extent of obtaining the "King's bounty" for them.
Unfortunately Mr. Oprey, who brought his English bride home after the war, died last July. Within a matter of days Mr. Sparling of the Kingston office of the Department of Veterans Affairs called upon the widow and found that she was entitled to certain moneys which had not been received due to an improper registration when the triplets were born. This matter was straightened out, and on August 4 of this year Mrs. Oprey was handed by Mr. Sparling a cheque in the amount of $201.37. Twelve days later, on August 16, a cheque for an additional $251.65 was sent the family. This was on account of the treatment the widow's late husband had had to undergo at Kingston. I understand a further payment will be made to Mrs. Oprey on the same account.
Furthermore, although this veteran's death was not originally attributed to war service, the case was reopened and Brigadier Melville, chairman of the pension commission, reported on September 5 that Mrs. Oprey had been granted a pension. This pension was allowed because of her husband's death -I am not a medical man so I shall have to read the cause of his death; it was due to herniation of nucleus pulposus of the sixth intervertebral disc, and although the immediate cause of death was pneumonia, it could be attributed to war injuries.
I am very glad to say that the pension has been made retroactive to the time of the veteran's death. The widow is now receiving $75 a month; plus $19 for the first child, $15 for the second child, $12 for the third child, and $12 for each of the triplets, which makes a total for the children alone of $82. Adding this to the $75 the widow is receiving, it amounts to $157. In addition to that she will continue to receive the family allowance for her six children, which, according to a Canadian Press dispatch, amounts to $31. Adding the $157 to the $31 makes a total of $188 per month. There may have been some delay in getting this for the widow, but I am proud and happy to tell this house how co-operative all the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs have been.

As I said before, it was only a matter of days before the first investigator arrived from the Kingston office. Ever since that time this case has been under the closest investigation, and it was through these efforts that the awards I have just mentioned were made possible. I am particularly happy that these awards have been made to this woman, because the rumour was getting abroad that Canadians were neglecting their new citizens from England. This should prove beyond a shadow of doubt that Canada does not forget those who served her in time of dire need, and there is no discrimination. I believe it also answers the point raised by the member for Fraser Valley when he said that these pitiful allowances are no incentive for men to enlist in the Korean brigade. Canada is known for her generosity to veterans and their dependents. This is just another example of the efficiency and humanity of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I should like to deal briefly, Mr. Speaker, with a matter which has been little discussed during this special session; in fact I believe only one question has been asked about it. It is the all-important subject of the St. Lawrence deep waterway. It was my pleasure and honour to accompany the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to Canton, New York, last June when he received an honorary degree from St. Lawrence university. Naturally, the Prime Minister was the speaker of the day, and during the course of his excellent remarks he made a strong appeal to the people of the United States about the number of years Canada had waited patiently for some kind of action on the St. Lawrence deep waterway that would fulfil the promise made to Canada so many years ago. The Prime Minister made his appeal not only to the graduating class of St. Lawrence university but also to the people of the United States, because his speech was carried on a nation-wide broadcast. It was particularly gratifying to sit in the audience composed of university students and graduates and hear the applause with which the Prime Minister's remarks were greeted.
I have lived on the bank of the St. Lawrence river all my life. Anyone who lives on the bank of that river cannot help but grow to love the mighty stream, and at the same time realize the potentiality of its waters which for so many years have been only partly utilized. Now that the whole world is in turmoil, and both Canada and the United States have been compelled to enact legislation concerning the allocation of certain materials for the production of munitions and supplies of war, I feel it is time to strike as hard as we can for the completion of this
The Budget-Mr. Fulford project. All one has to do is to pick up the daily papers of the last week and read the urgent requests made by the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission to conserve electricity, in order to realize how desperately this country needs further power development. There is no more beautiful view in this part of Canada than that which one sees from a point just above the city of Cornwall overlooking the Long Sault rapids. When one looks at that view, however, it is appalling to realize that between 216,000 and 260,000 cubic feet per second of water are going to the sea scarcely utilized. This water is capable of producing 2,200,000 horsepower of electrical energy, which would be divided equally between the state of New York and the province of Ontario. This electrical energy would go far towards alleviating the shortage that Canada and the United States are experiencing. It could be utilized to great advantage in the program of industrial expansion which will be necessary if Canada is to furnish the materials necessary for war. When I say "materials necessary for war" I do not mean to imply that it is war; it is materials for the defence of Canada and the north Atlantic nations which is the greatest guarantee that this country and the world have that there will not be war.
Apart from the power development of the St. Lawrence deep waterway, there are the tremendous potential manufacturing facilities along the entire great lakes system right from Prescott in the east to Fort William and Port Arthur in the west. Even today we see vessels passing through midstream of the St. Lawrence river, bearing not only the flags of Canada and the United States, but those of Norway, Sweden, Holland, and in one instance this summer even Iceland. These ships are performing a valuable, but not too economical service, owing to their limited capacity, in taking the goods of Canada direct to the ports of Europe. I have in _ mind one vessel in particular, the Prince Wilhelm III which makes Brockville a regular port of call, and which picks up anywhere from 10,000 to 20,000 cases of condensed milk.
The house will remember that a year ago I expressed some concern about the future of the evaporated milk industry in Canada. That worry has been completely dissipated. The evaporated milk industry of Canada is in a remarkably healthy condition, and I might say that part of that is due to the direct shipments that have been made from the ports of the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river to the ports of Europe.
I mentioned that operation of these ships is uneconomical. That can be understood
670	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fulford when they are limited to a length of 250 feet or thereabouts, and a total draft of 14 feet. Were the canals deepened and the waterway and the locks completed, ocean-going vessels of much larger size could penetrate to the middle of this continent, and the commerce of the world would be open to all tlhe great lakes ports of both the United States and Canada.
The point of immediate importance, especially because of our accelerated production for defence materials, is that of obtaining vast quantities of iron ore. Last winter we had the privilege of viewing moving pictures presented in the railway committee room by the Timmins interests. It was a revelation to all of us to see the vast extent of the iron ore deposits of northeastern Quebec and Labrador, iron ore deposits which some believe to be the greatest in the world, iron ore deposits which could and must replace the dwindling deposits of the Mesabi range in the state of Minnesota.
Canada is still obliged to import large quantities of iron and steel. We could be absolutely independent of the world if we could take this iron ore from Labrador and northeastern Quebec to our smelters on the great lakes. True, some of this iron ore will find its way to the Dominion Steel and Coal Company at Sydney, Nova Scotia, but the vast flow will be to the west, up the great lakes to such places as have large steel industries, such as Hamilton and Sault Ste. Marie in Canada, and Cleveland, Ashtabula and other ports in the United States, for transshipment to Pittsburgh and other steel centres. Furthermore, this steel would be utilized directly not only for the manufacture of materials for national and international defence, but also to increase the production of automobiles, trucks, tractors and the shipbuilding industry of the great lakes, and could furnish in secluded waters all the inland shipping that would be necessary in the event of the outbreak of hostilities.
The point I have not heard mentioned is the possibility of bringing the crude oil of Alberta directly from Superior, Wisconsin, by the large tankers which now sail the seven seas, not only to Sarnia but also to the refineries now located in Montreal, which are dependent for their crude oil supply on the Portland, Maine, pipe line, the oil for which comes from South America, the midcontinent fields and the Far East. This would ensure transportation by tankers in waters which at no time would be submarine infested, and therefore would constitute a large safety factor which would be lacking, no matter where the oil came from, if the ocean-going route had to be depended on.


I urge the government ht this time to renew, with all the force at its command, the efforts which I know have been made to interest the congress and the President of the United States to put through the St. Lawrence deep waterway project as a vital necessity at this time if Canada and this entire continent is to increase its production to the maximum.
I had the privilege of standing beside the late President Roosevelt when he made his famous address at the Thousand Islands bridge on August 18, 1938, in which he referred to the waters of the mighty St. Lawrence as dividing the two countries, but he added, "They should in the near future serve as an ever-increasing bond of friendship between our two great countries."

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate we have had, particularly from the government side, a good deal of theory and a good deal of oratory designed to counteract the rising demand in this country for price controls. I hope that having said that, having characterized what has come from the other side as theory and rhetoric, I will not indulge in the same myself; for what I want to do is to deal with this problem of rising prices in very practical terms, and with reference to one particular group of people in our country. Having done that, I shall make the point that what applies to the one group with which I shall deal applies to a great many other groups of our Canadian people, indeed to our whole population.
However, before I get right down to cases I should like to deal with one of the rhetorical utterances made yesterday by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) when- and I think it was a peak that he hit-he said, as is recorded at page 630 of Hansard for September 12:
However, there is one characteristic about the Canadian people. They will not be pushed around needlessly. There is no sacrifice that the Canadian people will not make for their country once they are convinced of the necessity of it. But a Canadian has an instinctive abhorrence and revulsion against unnecessary regimentation, unnecessary pushing around.
Let me say to the hon. member, who is watching me like a hawk as I refer to his speech, that I agree with him one hundred per cent when he says that the Canadian people abhor being pushed around. Where he gets off the beam, however, is when he thinks that price controls mean regimentation and pushing around. The fact of the matter is that what regiments people, what pushes them around and also pushes them down, is the lack of controls which leads to high prices such as our people are experiencing today. The whole concept of our democracy is based upon the rule of law. The logical

conclusion of the position taken by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano is that we should not have the rule of law, but rather that we should have anarchy in our economic affairs. We have had too much of that, and the result has been economic tyranny during far too many of the years our people spend upon this earth. When we ask for the rule of law in our economic affairs, when we ask for regulation and control of prices, we do so because we know that ordinary Canadians abhor being pushed around by blind economic forces. We know they want freedom, and that they will not have real freedom until they have economic freedom, along with those other freedoms we prize so much.
I could go on in that vein, but I must measure up to the challenge I have accepted for myself, namely that of staying away from rhetoric and getting down to cases. The particular cases I wish to get down to are those of our old age pensioners. In particular I want to point out what rising prices have done and are doing to the standard of living of our older citizens.
I have before me the minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 2, of the special committee on old age security which met during the last session. This is the issue covering the sitting of April 18, 1950. At page 28 we find a most useful and valuable chart which was presented to the committee by Dr. Davidson, deputy minister of national health and welfare. The chart to which I refer is headed "Chart 'A'," and its title indicates that it is a chart showing the value of maximum pension payable from time to time in relation to changes in the cost of living index.
What the chart does is to indicate where the cost of living index stood in each year from 1927 down to the time of the issue of the chart; and in those years where the amount of the pension was changed, the cost of living index is given two or three times, as may be necessary. Then there is a column showing the maximum pension payable during those years. It starts at $240, or $20 a month, as it was in 1927. Then the various increases are recorded, first to $300 a year, then to $360 and then, finally, to $480.
The third column in the chart is the significant one, and is headed, "Maximum pension in 1927 dollar values". In other words this third column shows what the decrease or increase in the cost of living has done, in terms of real values, to the amount of money we are giving to our old age pensioners. The real value, for the purposes of this table, as prepared' by the Department of National Health and Welfare, is based upon
The Budget-Mr. Knowles the value of the dollar in 1927. Obviously the reason that year is taken is that it was in that year old age pensions had their beginning. I shall have something to say later on as to what would be the result if we were to take the period 1935-39 as the base.
At any rate the table shows that during the depression years, when the cost of living index declined, it had the effect, which we can all understand, of increasing the 1927 dollar value of the pension being paid to our people at that time. Similarly it showed that when the cost of living index began to rise, and particularly when it got above what it was in 1927, the dollar value of what we were giving to our old age pensioners began to come down.
I have studied these figures carefully, and I have done some work on them, the nature of which I will set out clearly. For example, I have taken the figures which are given in this table on an annual basis, and divided them by twelve, so that We may see them in monthly terms, which are more comprehensible. Similarly, whereas this table was given to us in April, and therefore had the cost of living index only as late as March 1950, I have computed what would ibe the figure with the cost of living index as it now stands, namely at 168-5, the figure for August 1.
As a result of doing this computation and converting the figures from an annual to a monthly basis, I find that when in 1949 by act of parliament we increased the old age pension to $40 a month, we actually gave to our old age pensioners, in terms of 1927 dollar values, not $40 a month but $29.67. I emphasize that these are not my figures. They are taken directly from this table furnished by the Department of National Health and Welfare. All I have done is to divide the annual figure by twelve, so as to produce the monthly figure. There it is: The cost of living index at that time, in the early part of 1949 when we made the change, stood at 161-6. Let me repeat that with the cost of living index at 161-6 early in 1949, the $40 we gave our old age pensioners was worth at that time only $29.67 in terms of the value of the dollar in the year when the old age pension started.
Since then the cost of living index has gone up to 168-5 as of August 1, 1950, which is the latest figure. The chances are that it is higher than that now. The result is that the cost of living has still further reduced the value of the $40 pension we are now paying as the maximum to our older people down to $28.46 per month in terms of 1927 dollar values.

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
There is nothing in the minister's budget by way of an increase in the personal income tax, but here are persons by the thousands who in effect are paying a tax because the cost of living is decreasing, by the dollars and cents I have given, the amount on which they have to live. I go one step further-I think I am quite reasonable in this-and I ask: What will happen to our old age pensioners if the cost of living index continues to rise? Suppose it rises to 175? I do not think it is out of the way for that to happen if the government takes no action to prevent it. The 168-5 index was for August 1, but here we are at September 13 and the index is probably over 170 right now. If that happens and if the government takes no action to control prices and the cost of living and the index go up to 175, the value of the $40 we are now paying as a maximum to our old age pensioners will go down to $27.40.
I should point out that the same thing is happening to the ceiling placed on old age pensioners' incomes. As hon. members know, and as was emphasized this morning by the answer to the question the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) put to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), there is a ceiling on the amount of income, including pension, of $50 per month. When the government set that ceiling in 1949 it was worth only $37.09 in 1927 dollar values. With today's cost of living index that $50 ceiling has a value of only $35.57 in 1927 dollar values. If the cost of living index should rise to 175, the ceiling would then be down to a value of $34.25.
It does seem to me that this is no time for theorizing against price controls, such as we had yesterday in the oratory of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. When you realize that in plain dollars and cents the standard of living of our older people is being depressed day by day, both in the reduction of the value of their pension and in the reduction in the value of the ceiling on the amount they are allowed to earn from all sources including pension, it is time to do something about it.
I should like to point out that in what I have been doing thus far I have been following the idea which was presented to us by Dr. Davidson on April 18 when he gave us the fluctuations in the value of old age pensions in terms of 1927 dollar values. Most of us are accustomed to considering changes in the cost of living or dollar values in relation to the base set by the bureau of statistics, namely, 1935-39. In 1935-39 the cost of living index was considerably lower than it was in 1927. In other words, the value of the dollar was quite a bit higher. I submit that

it would be a more accurate portrayal of the situation of our old age pensioners if we were to compute the value of the pensions they are now getting in terms of 1935-39 dollar values, that being the base period determined by the dominion bureau of statistics. Considered on that basis the situation is far worse.
Taking the 1935-39 base period as 100, the 1949 cost of living index of 161 -6 would make the $40 maximum pension which was then granted worth at that time only $24.75 in 1935-39 dollar values. It means that with the present day cost of living index standing at 168-5, the $40 we are paying our old age pensioners is worth only $23.73 in 1935-39 dollar values. Similarly if my prognostication is correct, if the government does nothing about it and the cost of living index goes up to 175, which may happen before we come back next year, that would mean that the $40 we are paying our old age pensioners would be down to $22.85 in 1935-39 dollar values. To carry that projection a little further just to see the arithmetic of it, if the cost of living index were to go as high as 200, then the value of the $40 we are paying our old age pensioners would be cut in half and would be worth only $20 in terms of 193539 dollar values.	.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) points out to me that I am taking the most conservative position possible in connection with this matter. Old age pensioners spend a large portion of their money on food, and the food index is considerably above the general index. At present it is up to 216-7. If I were to use that figure, or some figure higher than the general cost of living index, in an attempt to get at what is actually the cost of living for old age pensioners, it would be clear that the situation is considerably worse for our older people than I have shown it to be with the figures I have given.
Let me go on with some more of the figures I have. On the basis of the 161-6 index, which was the figure when we made the pension $40 per month, in 1949, the ceiling of $50 was worth only $30.94 in terms of 1935-39 dollar values. With today's cost of living index of 168-5 the $50 ceiling is worth only $29.66 in 1935-39 dollar values. Similarly, if the index should go to 175 the ceiling would be worth only $28.56 in 1935-39 dollar values. If it got as high as 200, the ceiling would be down to $25 per month.
May I point out an interesting situation with regard to the years during which price controls were in effect. We all know that price controls benefited the whole community, but as I have been picking out one particular group in which I am interested I

should like to go on to show what price controls did for old age pensioners during the war years.
I find that in. 1941, 1942, and a part of 1943, when the pension was only $20 a month- and it was really pretty bad that it was so low-nevertheless the value of the pension in terms of 1927 dollar values was always a little more than $20 a month. Similarly, when the pension became $25 a month, it was only $25, a shameful pittance if you will, but at least its value in terms of 1927 dollar values was always a little more than $25.
On the other hand, when the removal of price controls began in 1945 and 1946 the reverse became the case and the value first of the $25, and later of the $30, went down below the actual amount of cash being paid to our old age pensioners. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I submit the case is very clear that when we had price controls we protected the value even of the small amount of money we were giving to our old age pensioners. Now without price controls we are letting the value of a slightly larger amount of money deteriorate almost to the level of the smaller amount that we were paying some years ago.
I am glad to note the interest-and I hope it is that-that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is taking in my remarks. I have a notion that this sort of thing worries him. At least it should. I believe that it worries him to think that the amount of money that his department is responsible for paying out to our old age pensioners is being allowed to deteriorate in this way and our old people made to suffer beyond all decency and reason.
The moral of all this is surely very clear. There are of course two main conclusions to be drawn. On the one hand, I think it is clear from the figures I have given why the people of Canada are today asking for price controls. They are asking for them for the very reason given yesterday by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, that they do not like being pushed around and that is what blind economic forces are doing-relentlessly depriving our people of the standard of living they thought they had won,
I suggest that the case I have made for old age pensioners can be made similarly for every group on fixed incomes. It certainly applies to superannuated civil servants. It applies to those on the burnt-out pension and to those on disability pension. It applies to a great number of our people whose incomes are of that nature, and it also applies to the wage earners who know from experience that their wages, even when they get increases, never catch up with prices that are continually rising.
The Budget-Mr. Knowles
On this occasion, however, I have presented the case for one group. I submit that that in itself is sufficient reason for the government to change its position with respect to price controls and introduce the necessary legislation to prevent our people, and especially our older people, from being pushed around in this way, and to protect their living standards.
The other lesson that I think must be drawn from what I have presented to the house this morning is the need for early action with respect to the implementation of the report of the special committee on old age security made to this house on June 28 of this year. I want to pick my words very carefully in dealing with this matter, despite the fact that behind my words there is very deep feeling and determination. I do not want to say anything, or have anyone interpret my remarks as indicating anything, that in any way could interfere with the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference agreeing to implement the recommendations of the committee, as a minimum objective. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I think that unless some voices are raised pretty strongly the dominion-provincial conference may be influenced by the kind of irresponsible editorializing that is going on in some of the newspapers of Canada calling upon the government to defer the implementation of the report, and calling upon the people of Canada to agree to the deferment of its implementation.
I think most hon. members will recall that when this question came up on the floor of the house rather unexpectedly last June I did not hesitate to get to my feet-

-and say that, even though the report did not go as far as I wanted it to go, I felt that the job of members of parliament of all parties was to get behind the report and make sure that it was implemented, whatever the next stage might be. Certainly that was the position to take in the sense that nothing less will do; but I call to the attention of the government, and particularly the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the kind of propaganda that is now being put before our people in the editorial columns of some of our newspapers to the effect that because of the international situation the recommended changes will have to be deferred.
Rising prices, with their corollary of depressing the value of the old age pension, make it imperative that something be done about this matter now. In fact I would say to the government that the time within which

The Budget-Mr. Knowles the people of Canada will accept the implementation of only what was in that report will soon run out. When the report was tabled last June, conditions at that time seemed to justify a report of that kind, going only as far as it did; if nothing is done to implement it in a matter of months, by next year, with prices higher, that report will not be good enough. Many people feel that it is already time to revise the recommendations of the report, to raise the amount to at least $50 a month without any means test, and perhaps to make other changes.
I cannot urge the government too strongly about the seriousness of this matter, and as to the seriousness of the time element in the whole question. I notice that the trades and labour congress convention has before it, if it has not already passed it, a resolution respecting this matter. They are asking, and justifiably so, for $50 a month, whereas all the report asks for is $40 a month at age seventy free of a means test, and $40 a month from sixty-five to sixty-nine with a new type of more liberalized means test. Times are moving, and one of the reasons why times are moving so fast with respect to this matter is that the government has done nothing with regard to price control. I submit that when the government goes to the dominion-provincial conference this fall and this question is being dealt with, the government should make its position clear that the will of parliament was that that report-certainly nothing less -should be implemented without delay.
I point out that the recommendations of the report do not involve any increased burden on the provinces. The report indicates that clearly and gives figures in proof thereof. The report indicates that implementation involves finding additional revenues at the federal level to the tune of about $250 million a year. When that figure was discussed in the committee last year there were some who thought it was a staggering sum, and that the committee had to act responsibly about it, and it did. But when we came to this session and were faced with huge expenditures, the first thing that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was able to tell us was that conditions had improved to such an extent, and prices were up to such an extent, that the tax rates already in effect are going to produce $180 million more this year than he estimated when he brought the budget down at the last session. You know, Mr. Speaker, it is strange how huge these sums are when you ask for $250 million for old age pensions, but how easily this $180 million just turns up in the minister's speech. I think he should make a speech once a week if he can turn up money that easily.

The taxes he proposes in this budget are not very severe, after all, according to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. He made it clear that in his view they are pretty easy. They amount to some $59 million, which together with the $180 million that was found by the minister in the manner I have just indicated makes a total of $239 million. Right there you have an amount, found quite easily, almost equal to the amount it would cost to implement this report so far as the federal treasury is concerned, bearing in mind again that it involves no increase at the provincial level.
May I point out also that the minister has made clear that the taxation measures he now proposes would net in a normal year around $2,800 million, which is $370 million more than was proposed when the budget was brought down last year. That is an amount considerably larger than the cost of these old age pensions. I am not suggesting that we should take this money we are voting this session away from the defence effort and put it into the old age pension account, but I am suggesting that if it is possible to find this money so easily for the defence effort, it is possible to find it for such an important purpose as old age security.
I suggest also that these figures do not represent the total as far as the defence effort is concerned. We have approved commitments for future years, and we have the large sum of money we have voted for help to our western European allies. So all told it is pretty clear that the money can be raised when it is wanted. I know that is an opinion expressed every day by the man in the street. It seems to me that is a sound opinion, and I agree with it-that if money can be found for defence purposes it can be found for such an important matter as social security. I urge also that this is part of the whole battle on the ideological front. Indeed, if we are going to win the war of ideas, if we are going to convince our people that our democratic way is not something we should prize just because we have inherited it but that we really believe in it, one of the things we must do is improve our whole position with respect to social security. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said that in his speech earlier this session, and he said that this was a time to redistribute the load on the camel's back. With that we agree.
I would point out as well, to those who argue against the implementation of this report at the present time on the ground that it would produce an inflationary effect, that the recommendations of the committee called for the raising of that additional $250

million by taxation. As a matter of fact, though the committee could not agree on a precise recommendation, it did make suggestions as to how that money could be raised, namely, in the field of taxation on individual incomes and on employers or corporations. I submit that for any editorial writer to say that such a program would involve inflation means that he just has not read even the last chapter of the report. It might be argued that throwing new money into the stream to pay this $250 million would be inflation, though even that is arguable; but you cannot argue that it is inflationary in any sense at all when you take $250 million out of the economy in the form of taxes and pay it out in the form of increased old age pensions. That is just redistributing the load on the camel's back, and as a matter of fact it might turn out to be an anti-inflationary move; for the result might well be a draining off of some purchasing power now being devoted to luxuries, using it instead for the purchase of necessities such as food and clothing, which the Minister of Trade and Commerce tells us are in good supply.
So, Mr. Speaker, on all counts I am convinced that the time has come for the immediate implementation of this report. The figures I gave in the earlier part of my remarks would indicate the absolute necessity of this. As a matter of fact I submit that it is already too late for $40 a month at age seventy without a means test; it is now time for $50 at age seventy without a means test, and for a better deal for those sixty-five and up. I contend, as I have stated already, that the money can be found. We have shown that this session. I point out again that to argue that this would be inflationary is completely false in view of the terms of the recommendations made by the committee.
I believe I have kept within the position I indicated a few moments ago, when I urged that what I was saying was not to be interpreted by anyone as interfering in any way with the discussions at the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference. I feel rather that the kind of editorials that have been appearing in our newspapers might be read by some of those attending that conference, and that it is time other voices were raised to remind them that this parliament is behind the recommendations contained in the unanimous report of last session's committee. That is the will of this parliament, and the government should make that fact known to the dominion-provincial conference when it meets to discuss this whole matter.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have just one other point to deal with before I sit down. I am back to where I started in one sense, namely 69262-43J
The Budget-Mr. Knowles that I am thinking of some of the things said yesterday by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. This indeed was a supreme example of how rhetoric and oratory can be impressive even though one gets away from the facts. At page 630 of yesterday's Hansard the hon. member mentioned our complaining about the cost of living index standing at 168. Then he said:
Let us look at that for a moment. The 168 is based on what? It is based on the average cost of living between 1935 and 1939. Let us remember the conditions in 1935 and in 1939. In 1935 we had the worst unemployment the country had ever known. Even by 1939, according to a royal commission, seventeen per cent of our working force were without jobs.
He went on to say that prices were low then, but wages were also low. Then he said:
, There is not a Canadian worker I know today who would want to go back not only to the 1939 prices but to the 1939 employment level and wage scale.
He went on to say:
I think perhaps the time has come when the base should be brought more up to date.
The whole inference was that those of us who talk about the cost of living index are somehow trying to take the country back to the base period of 1935-39. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano knows better; but what he does not seem to be prepared to admit is that the cost of living index, based as it is upon the 1935-39 level, merely says that today it would cost 168-5 as compared to 100 to buy the same budget of goods and services that were acceptable to the Canadian people at that time. I checked this very carefully, by reading again about the cost of living index both in "Canada 1950" and in the Canada Year Book, and by talking with the dominion statistician about the matter this morning. It is very clear that the cost of living index is still based upon the same total quantity of goods and services that it was based upon in 1935 to 1939. The hon. member is right; our standards are higher. Today we think people should have more to eat, better clothes and better homes than they had in 1935 to 1939. If that is so then the real cost of living today, taking into account the higher standard of living that the hon. member rightly argues for, is not 168-5 compared to 100 but is probably well over 200. I agree with him on one point, that it is time we had a new base. I understand from the Canada Year Book that the dominion bureau of statistics is working on a new base. The point is that when you study closely the basis of the cost of living index, you find that the view of the man in the street-and the housewife in particular- is quite correct; the cost of living index is too conservative. The position is really far worse than those figures indicate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two references I should like to make, in view of the fact that we are now approaching the end of this session. One of them has to do with the meetings that are taking place during this week and the weeks to follow: The meeting of the foreign ministers of Britain, France and the United States; the prospective meetings of the twelve foreign ministers of the Atlantic pact countries, and the meeting of the general assembly of the United Nations.
We were brought here for the purpose of doing something to meet the situation with respect to the aggression that today threatens Korea and every part of the world. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is about to leave this country to confer with the foreign ministers of the other Atlantic pact countries; yet the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has indicated that this house will receive no further information at this time. Yesterday in the British House of Commons Mr. Churchill pointed out the difficulties and dangers in Europe. I am not going to read what he said; it was placed on Hansard last evening by the member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins). Mr. Churchill is giving full support to the Attlee government in the extraordinary measures that are being


taken in Great Britain. He has stated that the situation today in western Germany requires action now if the peace of the world is to be preserved. Amongst other things, he has called for two or three divisions to go to Europe from Canada.
The minister is leaving now to represent Canada at these meetings, but there has been no suggestion from the government as to what stand Canada is going to take. Within the last three days, namely, on September 9, the Christian Science Monitor has dealt with this matter. The article refers to a proposal to station between five and ten American divisions on the continent of Europe as the United States contribution to the North Atlantic treaty organization's defence forces, provided that Great Britain and Canada put additional troops on the continent as well. The article states:
The decision to send five, six, or up to ten United States divisions to France, if other treaty countries contribute their share, shows a real determination on the part of the White House to act that is reflected by both parties at the capitol.
What is Canada's attitude to be? Is this matter to be discussed in parliament? Are the representatives of Canada to go to this conference without any discussion or decision by parliament? Anxious as is anyone to go home at the conclusion of the session, I contend that if it was necessary to call parliament together to meet the situation in Korea, it is an affront to this house, with parliament now sitting, for the Prime Minister to say that our representatives will go to this conference without any statement being made to the house about the attitude to be taken toy the Canadian representatives. The Prime Minister may laugh, and by his attitude indicate that the representatives of Canada are to go to the conference without an expression of opinion from parliament, which surely has the right to toe placed in possession of the facts. The serious situation in Europe has been mentioned not only in the United States, but also by the former prime minister of Great Britain. All we are asking, and I -think we have a right to ask it, is that Canadians as a whole shall know what Canada's attitude is to be.
Yesterday, the member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) said that there were periods in two world wars when the United States was not at war when Canada was, and that is true. But today we are building up an international organization to prevent aggression, and Canada has accepted some responsibility in that regard. Surely, when aggression faces Europe-as it must, otherwise Mr. SEPTEMBER 13, 1950
Churchill would not have used the words he did yesterday-parliament has the right to know what the stand of Canada's representatives will be in relation to decisions which may well assure our defence against aggression for a period of many years.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.
