speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock I was referring to the situation in Europe as outlined by Mr. Churchill and had stated that I did not intend to quote his remarks. I now feel that a portion of them should be quoted so that I can found my argument on them:
Winston Churchill appealed in parliament today for "a European army of at least sixty to seventy divisions" to make "some sort of front in Europe." He was speaking in the debate on Britain's new three-year rearmament drive.
"We have to form as fast as possible a European army of at least sixty to seventy divisions to make some sort of front in Europe and to close what I have called the hideous gap in the protection of western Europe from the Russian communist onrush to the sea."
A little later on Mr. Churchill said:
If an army of sixty to seventy divisions can be deployed on our gaping eastern front, the greatest threat of world war in the next three or four years will be substantially diminished if not indeed removed.
This will undoubtedly give the western democracies the best chance of securing a return in the normal relationships of states and nations. Whether we shall have time or not no one can tell.
Finally he went on to ask for two or three divisions from Canada among others for Europe. In these words he again stated the gravity of the situation as it has been stated on many occasions in this house during the present session. The situation referred to by Mr. Churchill in these terms is such as to be not only grave but dangerous if the necessary action is not taken. He expressed the hope that if action was taken we might indeed be assured of peace over the years.
Having regard to the importance of the meetings which are about to take place I said this morning that parliament should not be adjourned without parliament being advised and Canadians being told whether or not Canada intends to act. Having regard to the challenge given by Mr. Churchill and supported by Mr. Attlee I ask whether Canada intends to act. At least we in parliament should know what will be the attitude of those who represent us at the important meetings that are about to take place.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs will be attending these meetings. Surely we
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker have a right to expect some indication as to what Canada's stand will be. When I say that I do not mean to imply that any other nations should dictate to us, I mean that parliament has a right to expect that the attitude to be taken by Canada's representatives be known. That is not asking too much. The view to be taken by the British representatives at these meetings is known; they have already expressed themselves. Before leaving the British House of Commons the members of the ministry indicated it. Why should we in this country, with parliament sitting while these events are taking place, be denied information as to whether or not Canada agrees with Churchill and Truman that it is necessary to have these divisions available in the interest of international defence, in the discharge of our responsibilities under the United Nations agreement and the agreement binding the Atlantic nations?
Why should we not have that information? Why should we adjourn at this time and be told to go back home, that all will be well; trust us to do what is right? After all, parliament has the right to say, parliament has the right to indicate, parliament has the right to be consulted on the decisions to be made on matters so momentous as these. Certainly we were weeks and weeks late in regard to Korea. Under the circumstances as outlined yesterday in the British House of Commons, we cannot afford to be late in regard to the situation in Europe itself.
Mr. Speaker, in asking the government to let us know what are the plans, what is the general purport of the contribution to be made by Canada to these deliberations? Certainly no word has yet been uttered in this house, so far as I can recall, except the general words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, which would indicate where Canada will stand on a matter so important as this.
After several days of debate, parliament has voted many millions of dollars, and has done it willingly because the Canadian people as a whole are anxious and desirous that everything shall be done. No one in any part of the house will deny that for several years, from 1945 on, we were in a state of apathy, brought on by the fact that we believed the possession of the atomic bomb to be our defence against any possible aggression. We developed a Maginot line
678	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker mentality. That mentality has gradually disappeared since it was generally realized that the U.S.S.R. now has an atomic bomb of its own.
There has been $1,500 million spent over the last few years, and little to show for it. Hundreds of millions of dollars are now voted, and there has been no suggestion on the part of any minister of the crown, except in generalities, that the wasteful expenditures that must have taken place in connection with the hundreds of millions of dollars that have been voted will cease, will end, once and for all, in this country.
Certainly the granting of further hundreds of millions of dollars will in no way change the attitude of those who are in charge of expenditures. Canada has little to show for the many hundreds of millions which have been spent. We ask, as the Canadian people ask, and as they have a right to ask: What is going to be done? What measures are to be instituted by the government to ensure the end of wasteful expenditures and ensure effective and efficient expenditures?
There has been no suggestion on the part of the government that any serious reduction in unnecessary civil expenditures is to be made. There has been only the expression of a pious hope that departments of government will be notified that they ought to reduce their expenditures. We in parliament have the right to demand that there will be a reduction in expenditures which are unnecessary and which are too often made. Again we have not that assurance. What assurance have we to carry back to the people of Canada that the present extremely high cost of living is to be reduced? What message have we to carry back to them that inflation is to be met? After all, it is the sixth column, and it does almost as much as the fifth column in destroying effective defence expenditure.
With the exception of a few powers granted to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and some powers in connection with consumer control, there is nothing that will meet the situation and answer the call of the Canadian people that something be done at once, as it is being done in the United States, to curb and to stop the results of inflation.
Indeed, an examination of the budget will show that one person has been forgotten, and he is the consumer. The continually rising cost of living, which over two and a half years ago we were led to hope would be stabilized at 145, has climbed up and up. While parliament sits, prices increase.
The problem of inflation we have not faced. The government has given no effective leaderfMr. Diefenbaker.]

ship in facing it. If it were giving effective leadership, steps would be taken to cut down civil expenditures. Over and over again, as in the British House of Commons, we in the opposition have asked for the setting up of a committee on estimates, to the end that<at this time we should reduce to the limit unnecessary expenditures.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano said yesterday that if it was a case of making a choice between chocolates and guns, there would be only one answer. That, in effect, was what he meant. We are to get $18 million or thereabouts in revenue in consequence of the imposition of the tax on chocolate bars. But how many millions could be saved in travelling expenses and living allowances? I am not going to name persons, unless anyone wishes to have them named. $22 million was expended last year in travelling allowances and expenses. I shall give the house a few of them: $8,360 salary; $12,000 allowances, $5,868.34 travelling expenses, and $528 removal expenses. That is one person. Here is another: $6,900 salary; $11,652 allowances, and in addition the Canadian people paid his living allowances. One of our international representatives received his living accommodation throughout the year, a salary of $10,000, and allowances of $14,392.
I can give the pages of the public accounts if anyone wants them. That type of expenditure is not justified. Canada of course has to keep up a certain standard as a nation, a standard in keeping with her responsibilities. Here is another: $8,000 salary; $12,936 allowances, $1,903 travelling expenses, and $2,870 removal expenses. On top of that there is living accommodation.
How many of these are there? Well, last year I asked this question:
How many civil servants or officials in the fiscal year 1949-50 received in addition to salaries and travelling expenses, living allowances in excess of $5,000?
The answer was that there were seventy-two with living allowances in excess of $5,000, in addition to being paid salaries and travelling expenses. Why not restrict such expenditures, unjustifiable as they are today? Give reasonable and fair allowances and expenses, but many of the seventy-two who are referred to in this return should not have been allowed such heavy expenditures. I suggest that if a matter of this kind were submitted to a committee on estimates we would save several millions of dollars without in any way detracting from the efficiency of government.
When I go back to my constituency I will be asked as other hon. members will be

asked: What did you do to stop profiteering? The only answer I can give is: We did not deal with it this time. How is it to be met? Certainly the situation today demands action. While profiteering does not occur in general, it certainly occurs in particular cases which will come to the minds of hon. members in all parts of the house.
What is being done? While the cost of living continues to rise, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has a committee sitting for the purpose of ascertaining why the Combines Investigation Act is not working as efficiently as it should be. Certainly nothing is being done to meet inflation; nothing is being done about profiteering.
Hon. members of the C.C.F. have moved an amendment asking that the excess profits tax be imposed. The plan has been ridiculed by one hon. member. Some years ago it was held up in the house by members of the government as one of the most effective forms of taxation to prevent injustice by those who would extract from the people of Canada the last dollar they could pay. Of itself it would not be effective in removing the profiteering referred to in the amendment. Other things are required in addition. Above all we need the assurance of the government, as represented by the Minister of Justice, that the Combines Investigation Act will be used effectively rather than sparingly and too often against those who are not responsible for profiteering to the same extent as others who are not being prosecuted.
I come to the matter of civil defence. This matter was discussed at the mayors' conference in Saskatoon. No one looks forward to the day when we may be subject to atomic attack but the possibility must be faced. The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) referred to this matter at length, but that subject we have not dealt with in this house. We do not know the attitude of the government. I realize that the administration of civil defence must rest with the provinces, in particular with the municipalities who would supply the necessary hygienic, police and fire administration, but the extra expenses, imposed by the necessity of preserving our towns should be met by the federal authorities.
Mention has been made on several occasions of the necessity of increased production. There is nothing in the budget that encourages increased production, except that the income tax is not being increased and there is but a small increase in company taxation. In the United States, under powers analogous to those being given to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, production is to be encouraged by means of pro-
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker duction loan guarantees. Every effort is to be made there to expand and develop hidden resources, and the production of copper, iron, zinc and other commodities requisite to the mobilization of the nation.
In this matter of increased production I suggest that something must be done for the western wheat farmer in connection with an injustice that is growing from day to day in the changing of grades. I have received one letter after another about the growing dissatisfaction of the Saskatchewan farmer with the system of wheat marketing. One farmer says that he has heard of several cases in which the grade has dropped as much as three grades overnight. The farmer will be receiving 35 cents less per bushel as an initial payment this year than he received last year, and a large portion of the crops has been affected by frost and drought. Grades are down. If we are to expand the production of wheat next year, which after all is the cereal food upon which our defence depends, there [DOT]will have to be a full investigation of this situation by the board of grain commissioners to the end that injustice in connection with grading will be removed and thereby the highest possible return secured for the farmer.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) dealt at considerable length with the necessity of decentralizing our industry; but have we heard anything about the subject from the government? During the last war industry was centralized in Ontario and Quebec, and to a lesser degree in British Columbia. The trend today in the United States is to decentralization. If there is to be expansion and development of industry on the prairies, power projects such as the one proposed for the South Saskatchewan river must receive the attention of the government.
According to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) there is danger of atomic attack on our industrial production. I have a report of a speech he delivered in Toronto, in which he pointed out that danger and indicated that he believed in the necessity of decentralization. This cannot be done unless there is the necessary power development. Power developments such as the one proposed for the South Saskatchewan river are necessary if there is to be an expansion of industry in Saskatchewan. By decentralization we could build up our economy and at the same time lessen the dangers of atomic attack.
I think Canadians as a whole are asking about the matters I have referred to today. They are asking: What is the plan? What is expected of us? Will profiteering be ended

The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent as far as possible? Unless inflation is stopped we shall have to reduce our standard of living and the production of the requirements for defence. Surely parliament has the. right to know what the government is going to do. The people of Canada have a right to know what their trustees intend to do in general. We gave the government during the last five years a blank cheque of $1,500 million to spend on defence. Having regard to that expenditure I wonder how many hon. members believe that our defence has even been partly secured? The attitude of the government has been: Give us the money and we will do the job. They had the money for three or four years and yet today we are fearful-I feel restrained from saying more -that all that should have been done has indeed not been done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those of us, and there are several, who saw last night the press dispatch reporting the speech made by Mr. Churchill in the House of Commons at Westminster and who have read the newspapers are not at all surprised to hear hon. members on the other side of the house echoing that speech and putting it forth as a great challenge to the Canadian people. I should like to suggest to hon. members opposite that they might take their cue from the headline covering the report of that speech in a newspaper with which they are not altogether unfamiliar. I refer to the Montreal Gazette. The headline in this morning's Montreal Gazette is:
Churchill hits U.K. defence plan.
Underneath there is the following:
Asks seventy-division European army; two or three divisions from Canada suggested.
It should not be forgotten that at the present time Mr. Churchill occupies in the House of Commons at Westminster the same position that is occupied in this house by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Drew). He is the leader in that house of His Majesty's loyal opposition, responsible to the electors of the United Kingdom. In this country it may be surprising to some, but I am sure not to very many, that decisions about the formation and use of Canadian armed forces are to continue to be made by the government of Canada, and by the House of Commons responsible to the electors of Canada.
The hon. member wishes to have some further information. I will say to him at once that the government of Canada at this time is not considering the raising of Canadian forces to dispatch to Europe as a deterrent to aggression in Europe, and has not before it any such suggestion from any of the governments of the North Atlantic treaty nations.

Some three weeks ago it had some suggestions from the council of deputies of the permanent members of the North Atlantic treaty nations as to the provision of arms and equipment for increasing the deterring forces in Europe with respect to any possible aggression against them there. Those suggestions were considered. The decision of the government in respect thereof was brought to parliament, and parliament has appropriated $300 million as an answer to that suggestion.
It should be realized that the planning under the North Atlantic treaty is being done by the governments of the North Atlantic treaty nations, and not by the opposition parties in those respective nations. Personally I do not expect that those governments will suggest that the armed effort of a nation of some fourteen million people for the purpose of deterring aggression in Europe should be twenty or thirty per cent of the armed effort of a nation of 140 million people. Nor do I feel they are apt to suggest that the best value to be obtained from Canada's contribution would be by sending men to Europe, and housing, clothing, feeding and providing for them there, rather than by using those men here to help in our production of arms and equipment for men available in Europe, whose need of arms and equipment is greater than the European countries themselves can meet.
I say that because it seems perfectly obvious to me that if we are to get the greatest possible effective strength in Europe for the money and resources we devote to national and international security, $300 million spent on the equipping and arming of men already in Europe, men who are there, who have to be fed, clothed and lodged even if they are not armed, is going to provide much larger forces than the expenditure of the same amount of money in raising, equipping, arming, training, feeding, clothing and sheltering young Canadians who would, under the present condition of full employment, have to be drawn from the productive stream of this nation.
The government's present plans with respect to its obligations to the United Nations or to the members of the North Atlantic treaty group have been disclosed to the country and to the house. If and when those plans are changed or enlarged the government will follow the constitutional practice of formulating the decisions here in Canada, and of communicating those decisions at once to parliament so that members of the Canadian parliament will also have the opportunity to discharge their responsibilities to the Canadian public. If and when the governments of the North Atlantic treaty group cease to have the confidence of their respective

constituents, the opposition parties in the United Kingdom, Canada or elsewhere, wherever that might happen, will then have the responsibility of doing the planning in their stead; but until then the role of opposition parties and opposition leaders will no doubt continue to be that of critics hitting defence plans just as hard as they can.

speechtext:
Politics first because politics is the art and responsibility of governing democratic nations. It may be that some opposition leaders find that politics does not do the kind of job they would like to have politics do. Nevertheless that is the democratic system, and the system for the maintenance of which this session of parliament was called. Obviously that does not mean that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is going to the North Atlantic council with a closed mind, and that the government is not ready to give the most careful and deliberate consideration to everything which may be proposed or recommended to make more effective the joint efforts of the nations banded together under the North Atlantic treaty. But our present view is the view that was expressed when the recent defence appropriation was before the house, that is to say, that the most effective immediate contribution Canada can make to the joint strength in Europe of the north Atlantic nations is the provision of arms and equipment which will enable the young men of the nations of western Europe to have effective means of providing security for their own homelands, and of building up their combined strength as a deterrent to aggression from any quarter.
Now I should like to deal very briefly with some of the other points made by the hon. member for Lake Centre. He inquired whether Canada believes with Churchill- and, he added, with Truman-that it is necessary to have these divisions available; I assume that is the two or three divisions referred to by Mr. Churchill. Well, if the question means, does the government believe with Mr. Churchill that these two or three Canadian divisions should be made available at this time in Europe, I will say to him that the government does not hold that belief. The government does not believe that is the 69262-44

Mr. Speaker, this house has been sitting since two weeks ago Tuesday. In the first two days we dealt with the bill having to do with the strike situation, which was the reason for our meeting here. Since then we have been dealing with national defence and the various measures brought before the house in connection with the situation that has arisen.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in a sarcastic tone and a manner utterly out of keeping with the events of the day, saw fit

to play up to those who want cheap politics instead of action, and got the applause he is accustomed to get from his servile followers, he completely overlooked the fact -that at a time when he was speaking with some measure of earnestness, and no doubt intending to mean what he said, he complimented the opposition on the spirit in which they came into this house; the opposition had made it clear that they were anxious to co-operate in every way, but that the extent of their cooperation must be measured by the degree to which the opposition was taken into the confidence of the government. Since that time neither privately nor in this house has the government taken the opposition fully into its confidence in respect of any important matter that we have had under consideration.
Just as an example, the Prime Minister and others have made a great show about their belief in parliamentary practices and their view that it is not in keeping with the traditional discussion of these subjects to go into secret session. When we suggested that we should be glad to have an explanation, which we have not received as yet, of any plans the government has to meet the commitments it has undertaken, it was stated that a secret session was not in keeping with our practices. This government they tell us believes in coming right out in the open. There must have been those who were interested in reading that only yesterday in Banff the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) addressed a secret session of the Canadian chamber of commerce, so that he could discuss with them some of our defence requirements. No secret session for the House of Commons in which the minister could place before the members the information to which the people's representatives are entitled, but a secret session for the chamber of commerce in which he could discuss the things he claims he is doing for the defence of this country.
This house has been waiting patiently to hear some statement as to the way in which the plans of this government are being made to use the forces of this country in some effective manner; and yet in that case, as in others, we have to read in the newspapers about the things that are being done with those forces. They are not announced in this house. So far as the performance the Prime Minister has just put up is concerned, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the suggestion was not made here, nor will it be made at any time from this side of the house or from any part of this side of the house, that this parliament should abandon any of its authority over any of the obligations it has to the people of Canada. On the contrary we are seeking to assert the supremacy of parliament over the

business of this country. We do not think this government should be constantly telling us that we do not know what we are going to do until we have been told by the United States what they want us to do. Whatever respect we may have for Mr. Churchill-and there are those who apparently have more respect for his views than the Prime Minister -no matter wha't admiration we may have for any man or for any individual, the business of Canada rests in this parliament. It is for this parliament to make decisions with knowledge of the facts; but we do not want to be told that the government does not know yet what it is going to do because some other nation has not suggested what we should do.
This afternoon we were told that the Prime Minister does not think it will be suggested we should use our forces in any other way. It is for this government, with the support of this house, to say what should be done both in the matter of defence and in regard to our participation in whatever collective obligations we undertake. But, Mr. Speaker, at a time when we are being told over and over again that the Prime Minister of this country is almost the father of this idea of collective security, we do not want him to disown the child.
Let us be quite clear as to what it is that the members of this house are asking in connection with the various subjects that are before us. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said yesterday it had been suggested by some of the members on this side that we wanted to see Canada an armed camp. There is not one word anywhere in Hansard, not one word outside of it, which suggests for one moment that anyone on this side of the house ever asked that Canada be made an armed camp. On the contrary, what has been asserted on a number of occasions is that we most thoroughly agree with the proposition that in taking such steps as should be taken for effective participation in defence of freedom, we should not assume such a burden as will threaten our economy. If we do that, we may actually lose a substantial part of the battle without having fired a single shot. It is because of that very proposition that the members of this house have clearly stated on different occasions that one of the duties of the government at this time, consequent upon its obligation to make effective preparation for national defence, is to take every step within its power to effect economies for the purpose of protecting the financial position of this country, upon which the strength and security of our people rest.
A number of methods, Mr. Speaker, have been suggested for dealing with the business
The Budget-Mr. Drew of this house. Those suggestions have been made in a constructive and conciliatory manner, but they have been rejected. Over and over again the Minister of National Defence has refused to consider the appointment of a defence committee to assist him. The government has refused to appoint a committee on estimates which could examine those estimates when they were brought down. Last spring the government refused to consider the setting up of a royal commission, similar to the Hoover commission in the United States, for the purpose of examining ways in which economies could be effected. The Prime Minister has said, and in this case one could perhaps not object to a device which is very simple, that the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was sitting on the external affairs committee, and although he was a member of that committee no suggestion came forward as to economies which could be effected. There are other committees, Mr. Speaker. There are committees on public accounts, one on railways and canals, and others which deal with various matters. It can be said that not one of those committees has made a specific recommendation for reduction in expenditure, but I hope that no one outside of this house will be misled by that statement. The members of this house know exactly why that is so. Under our rules there is no such thing as a minority report. The rules of this house call for a report based upon the majority decision of the committee. Many recommendations for economies were turned down by majority votes in those committees. Furthermore, those committees used their majority to prevent effective inquiry at any point where they thought an inquiry might be embarrassing to the government. This device has made committees ineffective which could have been extremely useful.
We have suggested that there should be committees which would have some freedom of action, something of the right to do a job which is accorded to the committees of the British House of Commons. I understand that in Great Britain the committee, on estimates is actually under the chairmanship of a member of the opposition, which enables it to bring before it those who can give evidence on any relevant subject. Sometimes it is only by the least important but most ridiculous examples that one can understand best how far these things go. The discussion today is one which relates to the preparations this country is making, or should make, to play its part in the collective effort for peace. That is the purpose, the preservation of peace. No suggestion that the only role of the opposition is to criticize-and it has been amply demonstrated in this session that that has not been the exclusive role of the opposition-nothing of that kind will get us away from the fact that the second of the two reasons for which
The Budget-Mr. Drew we came here was to examine, as the representatives of the people of Canada, the steps which have been taken to deal with this allimportant subject.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has sought to emphasize the fact that in the press report today of the speech made by Mr. Churchill yesterday in the House of Commons at Westminster, the first-line heading emphasized the fact that he was criticizing the government for their defence preparations. That is so. There was not one word in the speech of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) which suggested that this house was in a position which called for it to take its instructions from Westminster or from anywhere else.
But remember that this subject has been discussed not only at Westminster. Last Saturday it was discussed by President Truman when he said that the United States was going to increase the number of men it would place in western Europe as part of an effort, not of the United States but of the members of the Atlantic security pact, to hold back the threat of communist aggression there. In that speech he made it clear that the extent to which it would be possible for the United States to go would be measured very substantially by what it would be possible for the other members of the Atlantic security pact to do at the same time.
Canada is a member of the pact. Canada's position is more nearly similar to that of the United States than any other nation in the world. For that reason the people of the United States very naturally would be looking with interest to see what position we take in regard to the obligations we have discussed with them, not only as members of the Atlantic security pact, but also as members of the United Nations and as members of that unique association, the joint defence board of Canada and the United States.
The question as to how many men Canada should maintain, and the further question as to where those men should be, are undoubtedly questions of major government policy to be dealt with by the House of Commons after being put before the house for approval or otherwise. No one who understands our constitutional system could possibly challenge that. Nevertheless whether our role is to be one that is directed exclusively to preparation for the defence of the North American continent, or of participation in any of the wider efforts to stem the threat of communism, the fact remains that those with whom we are associated will want to know from us what we propose to do in connection with that over-all plan of defence.

The Budget-Mr. Drew
The question is not so much: How many men will go to Korea? It is not so much a question of: How many men may or may not ever be sent to Europe? The question is: How many men are we going to train for active service here in Canada as part of our joint responsibility for the collective preservation of peace. That is the question.
The importance of Mr. Churchill's statement is not in any way that it can be taken as something in the nature of a call to us to do a particular thing; rather, it is a statement as to what he, at any rate, as an individual, thought would be our appropriate part in that particular collective plan-an opinion based upon the greatest experience possessed by any man in the world today as leader of a nation in a time of stress.
It is only upon that basis that we can examine those words. But those words must nevertheless be tied in simply as evidence of what others with wide experience are likely to think our responsibility might be. They should be examined along with Mr. Truman's statement on Saturday, and with the report we already have, which appears to be sufficiently authoritative, as to what they are discussing at the meeting of the representatives of the Big Three in New York today.
We are informed, with all the appearance of reliability, that they are discussing now what the measure of defence will be that should be set up in western Europe for the one purpose, and the one purpose only, of preserving peace by holding back the communist threat-a threat not to Europe and to Britain alone but also to us, to the United States and to all mankind. That is what they are discussing, and that is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will be called upon to discuss when the ministers meet in a few days.
The Prime Minister in his remarks today has made a statement which it is difficult to accept as a final statement in regard to what will be done when Canada meets the other nations. Surely there is one thing all of us can agree upon: Whatever is done when the foreign secretaries meet next week, let it not be suggested that Canada is waiting for someone else to tell us what to do. No government has boasted more than this government of what it has done to assert at all times the doctrine of Canadian sovereignty. May I point out that the doctrine of Canadian sovereignty is not a new doctrine. It goes back many years and found its clearest assertion in the position taken during the first world war by Sir Robert Borden when 

he insisted that Canada as an independent nation must act on its own in all decisions that it made at that time.
We give way to no one in this house in our assertion of the belief regarding the complete sovereignty of this great nation of ours. But sovereignty is not simply a matter of refusing to take direction from Westminster. You do not gain sovereignty by asserting that you will not take any suggestion or direction from one quarter and then simply leave the impression that you are waiting to be told by Washington what to do each time a crisis arises in world affairs. That is a type of colonialism which none of us wishes to see implanted in this country when so many are still talking about a form of colonialism that disappeared in 1867.
This country must make its own decisions. I am sure that this country is willing to accept the obligations that have been imposed as a result of the decision of this government to be a full participant in the actions of the United Nations. May I remind the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and those associated with him that, far from seeking to take advantage of every opportunity to criticize, the fact is that in the effort that has been made to rank Canada side by side with the other free nations in the defence of freedom not one single voice has been raised on the side of the opposition against the complete acceptance by the government of its obligations under the charter of the United Nations. That was our position; that is our position.
But we ask that in dealing with these things the members of this house be taken into the confidence of the government, be told what we are going to do, be told what plans there are and that we as members should not leave here, we as representatives of the people should not be dispatched to our homes, only to learn afterward through the press or over the radio what our executive has decided to do, a decision which must have been made already.
Even at this stage of the debate, with information being held back which we should have had, I repeat what I said in the debate on the speech from the throne: that the Prime Minister will find full co-operation to the extent that he takes the house into his confidence. To the extent that it is informed and can be convinced that the work is being done, the opposition will support what the government does on every occasion and will seek to encourage support of those efforts whatever they may be.
We urged that there be a secret session of this house so that we could be taken into the

confidence of the government. Although that has been turned down I hope that in view of the experience the Minister of National Defence has gained in another tribunal, which although important has not the same responsibility to the Canadian people, I hope that in view of the new developments of the past few days the Prime Minister will consider the wisdom of having a secret session so that we may be brought into the confidence of the government and be able to go home to our constituencies as members of one team to urge the people of Canada to get behind plans that will really do the job.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the house for more than a minute in taking the vote but I must correct the record because of the reference made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). What happened was that the chamber had given notice of a symposium of their members with myself and some others, which was to be a closed session. This was drawn to my attention when certain members of the press said that they would like to be there, with the result that the press, and everyone else who wanted to come, was there. In order to ensure frankness of discussion on the part of members of the chamber of commerce, it was announced by the chairman of the meeting that the discussion would be off the record. So far as I was concerned, of course no information of a confidential character was given, and I was assured those present at the meeting, perhaps unlike members of the opposition, felt that they had received useful information about our defence work.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to become involved in a discussion of whether this particular advertising done by the Post Office Department was or was not good. All I want to say is that I believe the Post Office Department is a shining example of a public service operated in such a manner as to result in great benefit to all Canadians. At the same time I think that what has just taken place between the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) might be taken as an indication of what might

The Budget-Mr. Argue follow in a great many instances if the suggestion of the leader of the opposition were accepted by the government, namely, for committees of the house to make a detailed examination of the expenditures of all departments and ferret out any waste there may be. If the record is good, as it apparently is in the case of advertising being done by the Post Office Department, why should the government not want committees where opposition members could ascertain, and thus perhaps prove to the public, that there is not any great amount of waste, and by that means help the government in what it is doing?
When the average Canadian sees a budget of $2,500 million I think he is bound to assume that that amount of money cannot be spent without some waste. When apposition members ask for committees to investigate expenditures and are not successful in securing such committees, then I am afraid that the general public may assume that there is a good deal more waste in public services than perhaps is actually the case.
It has been said during the present session by members of the C.C.F. party on almost every occasion on which they have spoken that we support collective security, the United Nations, and Canada's contribution to the stopping of aggression in Korea. It has been said that we will support future action by the United Nations to stop aggression no matter where it may arise. Having said that, I believe I should say that I agree with remarks made by the leader of this group about Chiang Kai-shek's occupation of Formosa. He said he felt that the best thing that could happen to Chiang Kai-shek would be to have him kicked out of Formosa.
Almost every day one can see in the press that a great many influential, honest and wellmeaning people are concerned about the United States' unilateral action in sending their seventh fleet to the waters between Formosa and the mainland of China. As one who supports the actions of the United Nations, I cannot support unilateral action by one country which in any way may prevent or hinder the United Nations from taking necessary action. I believe that Canada, as was done by Great Britain, should have recognized the present revolutionary government of China months ago. I believe such action would have been to our long-term advantage, and of course we would have been recognizing something which is a fact. Therefore I say as to the future of Formosa that the United
Nations should make the decision, and that all nations of the world should abide by that decision.
When the budget is being increased by a large amount for expenditures that are necessary-and I am sure all of us wish it were not the case-the government should act at all times in such a way as to make its legislation as fair as possible to all sections of the Canadian people. I agree with those who have already said that the present initial price for wheat and the spread between the various grades will result in only one thing, a severe deterioration in the living standards of the western farmer. Of course no one knew that a frost was coming. A severe frost occurred, and it may be true that there have to be wide spreads between the frosted grains and the good grains in order that frosted wheat may find a sale on the international markets of the world.
I am not complaining because I am not qualified to say whether or not the spread between feed wheat and No. 1 hard is too great, but I say that, in view of the fact that western farmers' incomes will be reduced because of the severe lowering of grades, the prices of all grades should be increased. On June 5 last the members of this group moved a motion asking for $1.75 wheat for the next three years. Members on the government side of the house voted solidly against our motion and by doing so brought about its defeat. Even if that opinion were held by government supporters at that time, in view of the reduced prices as a result of the frost surely consideration now should be given to increasing those prices. I am receiving many letters from western farmers who not only complain about the reduced prices for wheat but are fearful lest the final payment of the five-year pool may not be-large. They say, and I agree, that the payment should be not less than 25 cents a bushel. That figure is supported by the rural municipal association, the united farmers of Saskatchewan, the united farmers of Alberta, the Alberta wheat pool and other farmers' organizations. While saying that, however, I want to emphasize that it is even more important to provide security for the farmers in the years to come.
Then I want to advocate that some changes be made in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, on the basis of the real emergency that exists because of the frost damage. That act is drawn on the basis of the crop yield per acre. If wheat yields eight bushels per seeded acre or less a farmer may receive payment; but with severe frost the eight bushels of wheat may equal in value only five or six bushels.
CMr. Argue.]

So I would ask that changes be made in the P.F.A.A. this year so the eight bushels will mean eight bushels in value and not necessarily just eight bushels in yield, in order that farmers who have suffered from severe frost may have a chance to obtain necessary benefit under that legislation.
I come now to this budget. I well remember that in the spring of this year, in the face of an unemployment situation with four hundred thousand out of work, the government informed us that they had abandoned their theory of a shelf of public works, that they were not going to implement their 1945 proposal to deal with unemployment. As so often seems to happen with this government, however, something occurred over which they had no control, and employment increased as a result of the tense international situation. But I believe this government are no better prepared to adequately deal with the situation we are facing today than they were prepared six months ago to deal with the very real unemployment situation then existing.
We remember that last session when members of this group advocated a universal old age pension of an amount that would give the pensioners a reasonable standard of living we were told it would involve such a huge sum that it would mean an impossible burden of taxation. The press across this country said we did not want a welfare state, that it would kill initiative and cost the public too much money; so the government merely set up a committee, as they do in connection with so many things of this kind. That committee brought in a report recommending a pension of $40 a month to everyone reaching the age of seventy, without a means test, with the federal government to pay half the cost of a pension of $40 to those between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine, with a means test. The committee estimated the total cost at $365 million. According to the committee's report, this year the government will spent $106 million on old age pensions, so if the report were implemented it would cost the Canadian people an additional $250 million. That was we were told an impossible amount for this government to provide last session for improved old age pensions.
Today we are facing a critical situation in the world. We in this group support the measures brought in by the government to improve our own defences and enable us to play our part in combating aggression. In this situation, however, with a little war on and the threat of a bigger war in the offing, the government now can do what it could not do last spring for the old age
The Budget-Mr. Argue pensioners. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) estimated that the tax proposals he was making would bring in a total of $189-5 million next year. Then he stated that since he delivered his budget speech last spring the government had received a windfall of another $180 million in increased revenues not forecast at that time. So the minister is getting $180 million he did not know he would get, and in addition is taxing the public to the extent of about another $190 million. In other words he has been able to find $370 million in the present situation. I want to say I am glad he has been able to find it; but in this situation he has been able to find fifty per cent more than he was unable to find last spring for an adequate old age pension.
I admit right away that this budget will not impose a crushing load on the backs of the Canadian taxpayers, but I am afraid it is placing emphasis on the wrong things, that it indicates the beginning of a policy which, if continued, will mean a crushing load on the Canadian people. I want to quote from the budget speech of the then minister of finance on September 12, 1939. Speaking about the inflationary method of financing, at page 139 of Hansard of that day Mr. Ilsley said:
It represents merely a thinly disguised scheme of taxation of a most unjust type. It throws a grossly unfair proportion of the burden upon the person of small or medium income, the wage earner, the salaried man and those who have savings deposits, insurance policies or securities of any kind whose value is fixed in money. It represents a complete violation of the principle of taxation in accordance with ability to pay.
I agree with Mr. Ilsley that inflationary methods of financing are a complete violation of the principle of taxation in accordance with ability to pay. The present Minister of Finance told us that of the $180 million windfall rather more than half was being brought in because of increased production and rather less than half through increased prices. I do not know how many million dollars may be represented by the word "rather" so I will say it is just fifty-fifty; that half the $180 million is brought in through increased production and half through inflation. From inflation we are to get $90 million which, according to Mr. Ilsley, is the worst possible method of financing. In this year's government revenues there is $90 million which in my opinion, since I agree with Mr. Ilsley, is an evil way for the government to finance its expenses.
690	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Argue Yesterday when the hon. member for Mel-fort (Mr. Wright) was saying that the government's actions were inflationary, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) interrupted and said this:
We are paying all our bills, and have a little over.
I am glad the government is paying all its bills and I hope it will have a little over, but even if it pays all its bills and has a lot over that does not necessarily mean that the actions of the government will prevent inflation. Whether or not inflation is with us can best be judged from statistics obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics and other departments of this government. In 1939 the Minister of Finance set out the evils of inflation. He said the government of that day would be prepared to fight inflation. For the eight months from January to August, 1940, the cost of living index went up 2-1 points. From January to August, 1941, the cost of living index increased 5-4 points. In October of that year the prime minister announced a system of over-all price controls based upon the period, from September to October. In other words in 1941 an increase of 5-4 points in an eight-month period was considered to be so inflationary that price controls were implemented. During the same period in 1950, from January to August, the cost of living index rose from 161 to 168-5, or 7-5 points. There has been more inflation in 1950 than we had in 1941, but in 1941 the government took steps to prevent inflation and in 1950 the government is taking no adequate steps whatever to cope with the present inflationary situation.
Inflation has reached the point where the ordinary people of this country cannot afford to continue the savings they have made in the past. Let us say that a person had $1,000 on the first of January this year, and decided to invest it in government bonds at three per cent. During the first eight months of this year that bond would earn $20. If the figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics in relation to the cost of living index are correct, and I have never heard anyone in this house say that they reflected a greater increase in the cost of living than actually took place, it means that the value of the bond drops $50. There are farmers in my area who could postpone perhaps the buying of new machinery, but they cannot afford to postpone such buying because the price goes up almost every month. To protect themselves they must buy goods as quickly as possible before prices rise.
It has been stated that there has been a great increase in instalment buying. I believe that one of the reasons for this is that prices 

are going up so fast that if people do not hurry and get the article at today's price, they will certainly not be able to afford it at next year's price. The government has done nothing to guarantee that there will not be continued inflation which will reduce the living standards of the old age pensioner on a fixed income; the wheat producer whose wheat prices have been lowered, the worker who is not able to get increased wages fast enough to keep up with the increased cost of living. My main objection at this time to this budget is that nothing is being done to guarantee that inflation will not continue. Some anti-inflationary steps have been taken, such as curtailing the amount of loans farmers may get for new implements; to make it more difficult for people to finance the building of homes; and to make it more difficult for people to buy consumer goods on the instalment basis. These are anti-inflationary measures, but they are aimed at reducing further the standard of living of the little people in Canada. They allow anyone with a large income to continue buying anything he cares to buy.
Another important failure of this budget is the fact that its financial measures are not on the basis of equality of sacrifice. In 1939 Mr. Ilsley said in his budget speech on page 140 of Hansard of September 12:
In imposing the new tax burdens which this policy will require we shall be guided by the belief that all our citizens will be ready to bear some share of the cost of the war, but we shall insist on the principle of equality of sacrifice on the basis of ability to pay.
I agree wholeheartedly with Mr. Ilsley's statement that the budgetary principle the government should follow is equality of sacrifice on the basis of ability to pay. This 1950 budget falls down completely when one judges it on that basis. It falls down first when one realizes that $90 million is going into the government treasury through inflation and through nothing else. I am sure that every minister of finance will admit that is the most unfair way of raising public funds. There has been an increase of 5 per cent in corporation taxes. The minister believes that will, during the remainder of this year, bring in $13,500,000. I want to say that I support that particular part of the budget. At the same time the Minister of Finance announced increased taxes on soft drinks, candies and chewing gum which he estimates will bring in $18 million of revenue during the present year; $18 million from the children of Canada, in the form of a tax on soft drinks and candies, and in the same period $4,500,000 less than that amount will be collected from all the big business corporations

in Canada. I do not like the tax on soft drinks; I do not like the tax on candies and chewing gum; and in 1949, just before the election, apparently the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did not like them either. On March 22, 1949, he said that these taxes had not been easy to collect. He also said that they are the least popular of all the so-called nuisance taxes. They are not easy to collect; they are unpopular; they are nuisance taxes; and yet when we are facing a grave international situation the Minister of Finance goes into that revenue field during the present year to collect $4,500,000 more than he is asking in additional revenue from all corporation taxes. I say that certainly that part of the budget is not based at all on the principle of equality of sacrifice or on the basis of ability to pay.
In addition to that there is the excise tax of $17,300,000. I think that tax, roughly speaking, is based on ability to pay, to some extent, at least. People who want new automobiles, sporting equipment, jewelry and so on should, in the present situation, be called upon to pay higher taxes. There is the tax on alcoholic beverages, an increase in the tax on spirits and on malt, both of which will result in an increase in liquor and beer prices. Increased taxes on alcoholic beverages are inevitable. If the country were facing a much graver situation than one can read into this budget, these taxes should be increased and increased rapidly. But I want to say that increase in taxes on alcoholic beverages is regressive. It is not based on ability to pay.
The Minister of Finance knows that today many people in Canada like a glass or two of beer once in a while. Of course a tax such as this means that it is being spread over a large section of the public irrespective of their incomes and irrespective of their ability to pay. They will pay $10 million on that tax and the corporations will pay $13,500,000 during the remainder of this fiscal year.
I should not like to criticize the budget of the Minister of Finance without suggesting to him something which might be considered an alternative. I do not profess to be an expert in financial matters. The Minister of Finance is an expert; but nevertheless I feel I can outline steps which could have been taken in this budget in order that it might have been based on the principle laid down by the Minister of Finance in 1939, namely, that as far as possible there should be equality of sacrifice on the basis of ability to pay.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance told us that we needed $189,500,000 next year in the way of increases from
The Budget-Mr. Argue taxation. I want to assume right now that the Minister of Finance was correct; that that is how much money we need. To get that money one of the things he did was to put a 5 per cent increase on corporation taxes. I would much rather have seen that tax 10 per cent. The Minister of Finance may tell me that an increase in the corporation tax from 33 per cent to 43 per cent would mean that business would be extravagant, that it would not be efficient, that it would not give the services in the future that it has given in the past and the services that are necessary. I do not think he would be right.

In 1949, just before the election, the minister announced a reduction in the income tax and

The Budget-Mr. Argue an increase in the exemptions. He estimated at that time that, by having brought these things into effect, at the end of the year it would mean a loss in revenue of $270 million.
I know that if these taxes were applied today they would bring in even more in the way of an increase than the $270 million, because production and incomes are up. So surely a small part of that reduction in income tax could have been placed on the higher income groups during the present session. Surely, the persons who are earning, shall we say, $3,000 or $4,000 or more a year should be willing to pay additional income taxes. If the minister would only bring back into effect 10 per cent of the loss in income taxes through the action in 1949 he would toe able to balance his budget, he would be able to meet all of these expenses and have a small surplus, without all of the regressive and unfair taxes that were brought down in the budget. I think that is the type of budget that should have been presented to the people of Canada during the present crisis.
Before I conclude I want to emphasize again that unless steps are taken to prevent a further increase in the cost of living, all that will result from this budget is that the little people of Canada, the small-income group, through inflation will be called upon to bear an unfair and unjust burden as a result of the government's financial policy. If the minister would implement price controls to hold down the cost of living, and to prevent further deterioration in the value of the dollar, then he could embark upon a savings campaign. I am sure the people would be willing to save money if they knew that when saving the value of their savings would be protected and that, in addition, they were helping the government and their country in the present situation.
I believe the corporation tax should be increased even further. The taxes being adopted in the budget mean that the man who must work for a living will pay increased taxation on a number of items. The tax on earned income is being increased, but the tax on unearned income, that is on corporation profits is in my opinion being increased by too small an amount.
I say the government has failed to take steps to prevent inflation, and has failed to bring in a budget based upon equality of sacrifice, judged on the basis of the ability to pay. The government has failed not only this year but in the years past to do for the people of Canada by way of improving social services and increasing social security those things that should have been done in peacetime, because it said the money could not be found.


It can find the money now in a time of crisis for purposes of defence and to prevent aggression. It should not hesitate even now to find like or even larger sums to implement needed social security measures.

Mr. Speaker, after the outburst of oratory that rocked the rafters of this chamber this afternoon, as a humble backbencher I hesitate even to rise in my place. However, I should like to say a word of congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for the excellent budget he brought down the other evening. I say that on behalf of the people of my constituency, who consist chiefly of little people who, because of the seriousness of international events had been anticipating that more would have been taken from their pockets than had been formerly, in order that they might meet their obligations as citizens of this country.
I cannot say that I am entirely in accord with everything that was brought down in the budget. I did hear that my little four-year-old was busy circulating a petition among his playmates, with the intention of sending it to the Minister of Finance in vigorous protest against the imposition of the additional tax on soft drinks.

My principal reason for rising was to reiterate in part some of the remarks of my neighbour in New Brunswick and my very good friend, the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). He pleaded with the government and particularly with the Minister of Trade

and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to encourage where possible the decentralization of industry.
In that connection I should like to read into the record an editorial which appeared under date of August 14 in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal, one of the leading newspapers in eastern Canada, and, it goes without saying, which enjoys the widest circulation in my province. I believe that through the good offices of the Saint John board of trade this editorial found its way into the mail boxes of all members of the House of Commons. I should like to place at least this part of it on the record:
It is earnestly to be hoped that authorities will heed this resolution-	.
The reference is to a resolution passed by the maritime board of trade.
-and that this part of the country will get a better deal than was the case during the second world war, when industrial expansion was concentrated in Ontario and Quebec. The policy of putting nearly all war plants in those two provinces was extravagant and harmful.
Among other things, it involved moving thousands of workers from the seaboard to the interior, where new housing had to be provided for them. It also placed an added burden on the railways, which had to transport military supplies from central Canada to Saint John and Halifax for shipment overseas. (Had more of these supplies been manufactured in coastal centres, the strain on the railways would have been eased.)
On top of that, the fact that so many factories were located in central Canada, and practically none in the Atlantic provinces, led to post-war economic problems.
These factories, after the conflict ended, were turned to the production of civilian goods, and brought Ontario and Quebec the greatest wave of industrial growth in their history. The eastern provinces were in no position to share in this. When a company could get a ready-made plant in Ontario or Quebec for a fraction of what it would cost to build one, it was certainly not inclined to consider operations in provinces where no such plants were available.
It is clear now that in the next few years Canada will spend hundreds of millions of dollars on rearming. The Russian threat makes this imperative. With this program in the offing, the government has an opportunity to take practical steps to decentralize industry and to lay the foundation for sound future prosperity in the seaboard region.
I would commend that editorial to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the other members of the cabinet.
May I also make reference to a resolution which has been or will be passed by the Canadian chamber of commerce at its present meeting. The resolution was to have been initiated by the Saint John board of trade, and reads:
We urge the Canadian government, as a matter of paramount importance, that immediate steps be taken in the face of the rearmament program and the mobilization of Canada's industries, to see that
The Budget-Mr. Riley they be decentralized both in relation to available manpower and in the face of the probable additional hazards to the larger centres of new global strategy.
That resolution was passed by the Canadian chamber of commerce at the locus referred to by the leader of the opposition as the locus of the mystical, imaginary and secret session which took place in the presence of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton).
I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and members of the government to the fact that our problem in the maritime provinces is a serious one. I realize that I may be regarded as rethreshing an old crop, that it may be considered as a plaintive howl from a maritimer, as something that is heard so often and referred to so disdainfully in other parts of the country, but I believe that something can be done to bring about economic progress in the maritime provinces.
If the government could see fit to allocate contracts to industry in the maritime provinces and to encourage the founding of new industries to use the raw materials that are available or close by, it would stimulate the growth of those provinces. It would encourage our young people to stay at home and not go to other parts of the country or to other countries in an effort to obtain security for themselves and their families. If some of the large munitions plants in central Canada were broken down a bit and part of the operation carried on in eastern and even in western Canada, the central parts of Canada might not be faced with the problem of unemployment which is likely to arise in the future when work cannot be found for the influx of labour which had come from the eastern and western sections of Canada during a period of abnormal prosperity brought about by periods such as we are about to enter into.
I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is alive to this problem and is constantly endeavouring to find a solution for the difficulties faced by the maritimes. I ask him to give impetus to any program he may have in mind along these lines. I am encouraged by the knowledge that in looking around the country for a place to spend a holiday the Minister of Trade and Commerce decided upon St. Andrews-by-the-sea in the constituency of my good friend, the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). It was with keen pleasure that the people of my province learned that the minister had purchased a home in St. Andrews. He is simply following in the footsteps of great men like

The Budget-Mr. Riley Franklin D. Roosevelt, who spent many holidays at Campobello island, also in the constituency of Charlotte. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was also attracted to our province last summer when he spent an enjoyable time in the constituency of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Richard).
There is one problem which is common to both the hon. member for Charlotte and myself, the problem that faces the fishing industry. I do not want the house to think that I am introducing a subject which is not equal in importance to those that have been dealt with during this session. I feel, as does the hon. member for Charlotte, that the fishing industry in Saint John-Albert and Charlotte in New Brunswick is dangerously close to extinction. We maintain that it is of national importance that the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Public Works should give encouragement to the fishing industry and to fish processing programs.
Before coming to Ottawa I had the privilege of attending a number of meetings called by fishermen in my constituency who told me that in the bay of Fundy, particularly in Saint John county, the young men do not want to take up fishing because it is impossible to find safe harbours during stormy weather. I urge the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), as I have urged his officials in the past, to take cognizance of the fact that the fishing industry in that section of New Brunswick is an integral part of our economy and there must be safe harbours for the fishing craft if they are to land their catches from the bay of Fundy.
The breakwater at Lorneville in my constituency has completely disintegrated while at Chance Harbour the breakwater is inadequate to provide the required protection from the heavy seas of the bay of Fundy. Those seas tend to become heavy at various times during the year. Plans have been drawn up indicating splendid breakwaters to be built for these fishermen, but they have waited year after year and nothing has been done.
I urge the Minister of Public Works not to attempt to economize to the disadvantage of the fishermen of Chance Harbour and Lorneville in my constituency.
I realize that economies must be effected in order to make more money available for national defence, but there are certain programs under way in respect to the harbour facilities at Saint John which should not be overlooked when an endeavour is being made to cut down expenditures. Saint John is always an important harbour in time of war for the transportation of men as well as


materials and everything possible should be done to keep its harbour facilities in the best condition possible.
I had intended to speak for only five minutes when I coaxed Mr. Speaker to recognize me but, as I said before, the oratory which preceded me simply carried me away.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). Before speaking on the subject matter of the amendment to the amendment, the imposition of an excess profits tax, I want to deal briefly with the present budget with relation to the subject of inflation. In recent years it has been generally recognized among economists that a budget is something more than just a means for raising revenue. In Sir Stafford Cripps' budget speech last spring I think he stated the purpose of a modern budget when he said:
The budget itself can be described as the most important control and as the most powerful instrument for influencing economic policy which is available to the government.
My criticism of the budget before us now is that it reverts to the sole purpose of raising money. The minister appeared to me to have completely disregarded the power, which could have been exercised through the budget, to check inflation, and has contented himself with the raising of the few millions extra needed for our defence. The budget, in my opinion, ignores completely the fact that we are in the midst of a period of inflation, an inflation that is certainly greater than anything the minister or the government expected when they embarked upon their decontrol policy, an inflation that is certainly much greater than the one which brought about various price controls in 1941.
Members of the house have already compared the cost of living at that time with the cost of living today, and have submitted ample proof that there is a much greater degree of inflation in Canada today than there was when the government took those steps in 1941. Before the final vote is taken on the budget I should like to hear from the minister just how he thinks the new taxes contemplated by the budget will affect the rising cost of living, and just what effect these hew taxes will have upon inflation in this country. I do not think the tax on chocolate bars and soft drinks is intended to check inflation. I do not think that a 5 per cent increase in corporation tax is going to be sufficient to curb seriously profiteering on war materials, or to prevent a further rise in the cost of living. I do

not think that the additional excise tax on spirituous liquors is going to result in any decrease in their sale.
It seems to me that no measures have been submitted by the government at this time, either in the budget or in any of the bills placed before us, that are designed to check inflation, or that give any indication that the government is fully conscious of the serious nature of inflation today. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) referred to the present inflation as an incipient one. I wonder how much he wants the housewives of this country to pay for meat, coal, boots and shoes, and clothing before he recognizes an inflationary condition. I seriously suggest that the Minister of Finance consult Mrs. Abbott on this matter instead of some of his present advisers, whoever they may be.
The budget which we are called upon to approve will remain in effect until March 31, 1951, more than six months from now. In my opinion it gives the "go" sign for an open season in profiteering and inflation from now until the next budget is introduced. It is true, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) suggests, that we may be spending only 10 per cent of our national income on defence measures instead of the 40 per cent we spent during the war years, but whether we spend 10 per cent or 40 per cent the cold, hard fact is that we have today an inflation which is more serious so far as the mass of the people of the country are concerned than the inflation in 1941 which was met by control measures. It is true, as the government suggests, that we may not actually be engaged in war. We may only be spending money on defence measures on our way up the hill of difficulty on the road to peace to which the minister referred. The fact is that we are going to require the concerted efforts of our people to make those measures effective just as we would if we were actually engaged in what the government would consider a war.
The former prime minister, the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, had some very good things to say about the evil effects of inflation upon the country in 1941. He gave us his views in a classic broadcast he made in October of that year. I think it would be good for the soul of the Liberal party if they would re-read some of the things that their former leader had to say on that subject, and take them to heart. I am sure it would be worth while for the minister and the country to recall some of his statements. I am going to refer to what he said in the broadcast at some length. I shall quote from a report of the broadcast which appeared in the Montreal Star of Monday, October 20, 1941. I give these references because I think they are
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy quite relevant to the present-day condition. Among other things Mr. King had this to say:
It is scarcely necessary for me to say that a rising cost of living is a source of acute personal anxiety to all and, particularly, to those with small incomes. And it is this very anxiety which is the danger to our war effort. For in the making of war no weapon is more powerful than peace of mind.
We all know that we cannot do our best work and put forth our utmost effort if we are beset by personal fears and anxieties. And we know that a maximum effort for Canada depends upon each and all working together in conditions that are just to all. That is why the government, which is responsible for the direction of Canada's war effort, is deeply concerned about the effect of rapidly rising prices upon the prosecution of the war. That is why the government has decided that hereafter prices must be controlled more rigorously than they have been during the first two years of war. The needs of today demand it.
In passing I want to say that in my opinion the needs of today demand rigorous measures of price control, just as much as did the conditions of 1941. During that broadcast Mr. King quoted a statement by the secretary of the treasury of the United States, which it would be well to keep in mind today:
Only the profiteer, the speculator and the hoarder gain from inflation.
I think one might add that the Minister of Finance sometimes has a budgetary gain from inflation, since this year he expects to get $90 million as a result of this condition. Then the prime minister of that time went on to say:
Rising prices and a rising cost of living do not have the same effect on all households. The smaller the family income and the larger the family, the more serious the hardship imposed. For those with small incomes, rising prices of clothing, goods and other necessaries may mean serious hardship, while for those with larger incomes only luxuries and small comforts may have to be given up.
I suggest that this statement represents a different attitude toward the interests of the common people of this country than that expressed in the budget now before us. Some hon. members have asked whether industrial workers would approve the imposition of controls, and this is what the former prime minister had to say in that connection:
Rising prices thus serve to aggravate the inequalities in society, and to throw the heaviest burdens on those least able to bear them. Wartime experience has shown that prices rise faster than wages or salaries-
That is a fact we sometimes forget; prices rise faster than wages or salaries.
-and bear more heavily still on those who live on small pensions or life savings.
So the leader of the government of that day was concerned with the industrial worker, in contrast to the attitude of the present government.

I want to give another quotation with respect to wages:

suffer more than the relatively well-to-do.

Nor is the position of the farmer any happier than that of the wage earner. The present war is a war of machines.
