The rise in prices will consequently be unequal, if prices are left to themselves. The things farmers have to buy tend to go up in price more than the things they have to sell.
I am going to give just one more brief quotation which I think applies to the present government. Speaking of inflation Mr. King said:
I think I have said enough to make it clear why the government is unwilling, as a means of reducing consumption, to allow prices to rise unchecked. That would be the easy way out of the immediate difficulty.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that today the Minister of Finance and the government are following that easy way out of the difficulty now confronting the country. They are taking the course of least resistance, the do-nothing course, the easy way which Mr. King referred to in 1941 as the way the government of that day was not prepared to go. I submit that today, though we may not be at war as we were in 1941, and though we may not be spending forty per cent of our national income on defence as we were then, the question of inflation, rising prices and the cost of living is just as serious to the Canadian people as it was then, and that it can interfere with any united effort to build up our defences against communism just as it would have interfered with our allout effort in 1941. I believe any government concerned with the welfare of the people would be taking measures today to protect their welfare and avert the evils of inflation, similar to the measures the King government took in 1941. Unless we want to adopt a policy of appeasement, such as gave Hitler his head start in Germany in the last war, the international situation can soon become just as grave as it was in 1941.


Altogether apart from the international situation and its gravity, however, I believe the domestic situation in respect to inflation is just as threatening today as it was in October, 1941.
Does the minister for one moment believe that industrial workers will, when this parliament adjourns with the imposition of a budget which does nothing to check inflation, sit on the sidelines and watch prices continue to rise? Does he believe these workers will be content to watch the purchasing power of their pay envelope become less and less? There is not a trade union leader in this country who would be worthy of the position he holds if he were to sit idly by and watch the process of profiteering continue in this country, watch the purchasing power of the pay envelope become less, without taking measures to effect an increase in wages for his workers. Mr. King well understood that situation. He knew that in times of inflation prices will rise before wages, and that wages cannot keep up with the spiraling staircase of inflation. I have not any doubt but that this budget, and the government's refusal to face up to rising prices, will result in the recurrence of interruptions in production; the recurrence of demands for increased wages from trade unions all across this country. With all the discontent among our people, such a situation is the result. It is for reasons such as these that I, and those in this group, have been insisting that price controls and excess profits taxes should be reimposed at this session.
There are a few things I want to say, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of excess profits taxes. I have carefully read the reasons the minister gave for not imposing excess profits taxes at this time. He gave three reasons, and they are to be found on pages 422 and 423 of Hansard for September 7, 1950. The first reason was that, to be effective and fair, an excess profits tax must be based on a comparatively recent period. He suggested that if such a tax were based on the last three years not much revenue would be collected because profits had been so high. I agree with the minister that an excess profits tax must of necessity be based on a recent period in order to tax the more recent expansions in industry and new industries which have grown up in recent times. It is, however, by no means necessary for the government in adopting, say, the past three years as the base, or any one of the past three years, to exempt' one hundred per cent of the profits made in those three years or in any one of those years. The government may

fix a ceiling of any percentage of profits it chooses which, in its opinion, would be fair and equitable.
It is true that the past few years have not been normal years. Business in this country has had a field day during the past few years. This has been due to the need for reconstruction in Europe, Marshall aid, and relatively high peacetime expenditures on defence. All these things have contributed to high profits for business in that period. In the light of that, I submit it would not be necessary for the government to fix a ceiling which would exempt one hundred per cent of the profits made in those years. There was some justification for exempting one hundred per cent of the profits made in the base period when the previous excess profits tax was put into effect. The base period represented an abnormal time, because it was immediately following the depression when business was not good. Many small businesses, particularly, had not recovered from the depression, and as a result there were many inequalities. The government was probably justified in exempting one hundred per cent of the profits made in that base period, and placing an excess profits tax over and above the one hundred per cent. These arguments, I submit, do not apply to the past three years with which we are dealing.
The minister's second reason was not particularly complimentary to corporate management. His statement was to the effect that the excess profits tax would encourage waste and extravagance on the part of corporate management. I quite understand that corporate management would expect a statement of that kind from a C.C.F. speaker.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was examining the objections which the Minister of Finance raised to the imposition of an excess profits tax at this time. I agree with the minister's contention that an excess profits tax should have as its base a recent period of time; it should probably be based on the years 1947, 1948 and 1949. I disagree with the minister in his statement that because profits were so high in those years no excess profits could result in taxes to the government from such an act. My contention was that it was by no means necessary for the government, in taking this base period, to exempt a hundred per cent of the profits made during those
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy years from taxation before imposing an excess profits tax. The government could take as its ceiling any percentage of those profits which it considered fair and equitable.
In the light of the favourable conditions under which business operated during those years, conditions arising out of post-war needs, I feel it would be quite equitable for the government to place that ceiling at much less than one hundred per cent of those profits. If we look at the profits made during those years and compare them with previous years I think we can see where the government, without interfering too much with corporate business, could levy a tax of at least $200 million or $250 million.
Corporation profits before taxation in 1944 amounted to $1,221 million. Of that $1,221 million we collected in taxes $603 million, or approximately fifty per cent, leaving $618 million of profits after taxation. In 1949 we had a very different picture. In that year corporation profits amounted to $1,914 million. In that year we took only $673 million in taxes, only $70 million more than we took in 1944. In other words, where in 1944 we took fifty per cent of corporate profits in taxation, in 1949 we took only about thirty-three per cent in taxation. In that year out of the $1,914 million in profit we left $1,241 million to corporation shareholders in profits after taxation. I feel that there is room for an excess profits tax that would bring to this country at least $200 million or $250 million.
The second objection which the minister raised is, as I mentioned, before six o'clock, not very complimentary to corporate management. He says an excess profits tax is an invitation to extravagance and waste in corporation management. As I pointed out before six o'clock, I have no doubt corporate management would not be surprised to find C.C.F.'ers offering such a criticism as that. I am sure corporate management must have been a little surprised to find such a criticism coming from the Minister of Finance of a government that has had considerable experience in administering an excess profits tax. Are we to understand from the minister's statement, and from one who ought to know, that corporations will slacken on the job of production when there are no profits in sight, even though their country is taking those profits for the protection of free enterprise against communism? Are we to understand that corporate management will slacken on the job of production when every housewife in Canada, when every child in Canada, is already suffering from the
698	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy evil effects of inflation? That I submit, Mr. Speaker, is a statement which even a C.C.F.'er finds very hard to believe.
Surely our great captains of industry, those great supporters of our free enterprise system, those to whom the defeat of communism means so much, surely those men have more patriotism and humanity in their business dealings than the minister would have us believe.
The minister's third objection was that an excess profits tax at this time would, as during the war years, work severe inequalities. He leads us to believe that it is almost impossible to impose an excess profits tax that will not create these inequalities in business. I will agree with the minister that there were a great many such inequalities under the old Excess Profits Tax Act. I think those inequalities arose from the fact that the period which was taken as the base period for the administration of that act was an abnormal one. Those were years following the depression, years in which a great many small businesses in the country had not recovered sufficiently from the depression to have arrived at any stage of profit.
These conditions do not apply to the years 1947, 1948 and 1949. I am confident that an excess profits tax with those years, or any one of those years, as a base period, would not inflict the same severe inequalities as were experienced under the old act.
In concluding I should like to quote two short passages from the former prime minister. First I shall quote from a published address of his delivered in Toronto on March 24, 1941. The address is entitled "A New World Order". We heard a great deal about that new world order during the years of war. I shall now read to the house the new world order visualized by Mr. King.
First perhaps it might be well to refresh our memories as to what we were talking about in the early forties. This paragraph is headed "A New Heaven and a New Earth" and is in these words:
A new heaven and a new earth-are not these, in very truth, what we seek today? A heaven to which men and women and little children no longer will look in fear, but where they may gaze again in silent worship, and in thankfulness for the benediction of the sun and the rain; an earth no longer scarred by warfare and torn by greed, but where the lowly and the humble of all races may work in ways of pleasantness, and walk in paths of peace.
Mr. King went on to point out that this new order found expression when Britain determined to put an end to aggression in Europe in 1939. It found1 expression when the nations of the British commonwealth took their place at the side of Britain, and in the 

resolution of the United States of America to lend its powerful aid to the nations which were then fighting for freedom.
Mr. King did not foresee in 1941 that in less than ten years it would become necessary for the freedom-loving nations to oppose aggression by force. In that address he made one prophetic statement, the truth of which may be seen today, when he said:
If that new order is not already on its way before the war is over, we may look for it in vain.
How true were those words. We have only to look back in order to realize to what extent we failed to secure the beginning of that new order before the war was over. We may today be on the verge of another titanic battle between the free nations of the world and another dictatorship. We shall need in that struggle, as in the last, all the united effort our people can put forth. That united effort in this country will depend upon the government's success in removing from all Canadians the personal fear and anxiety which rising prices, with their trend of profiteering, hoarding and speculation, create.
So far we have very little indication from the government, either in this budget or in any legislation presented, to show that it is at all cognizant of the dangers inherent in the present economic situation.

I think, too, that the only reason the budget was brought down was that it was necessary to maintain our Canadian peace and security which has been threatened by international communist imperialists. It is my firm belief that the danger is real, not fancied. Any intelligent person who can read can see that the forces of darkness and evil have combined themselves with Russian communism and have become so powerful that they are forcing the rest of the world to waste their

efforts in the building up of armed forces strong enough to fight against aggression.
I saw service in the last war, and I know something of what war can do. I, and I think all the men who served with me during the war, hate war. At the end of the last conflict I had hoped that Canadian youth would never again be asked to take up arms anywhere in the world. But, much as I hate war and all that it stands for, I love my freedom much more. And so, because the main aim in the budget is to raise money to prepare Canada against any active aggression, as well as to discharge our obligations to the United Nations, I feel I must give my general support to the efforts of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) at this time.
At the same time however I feel I must be critical of the government's failure to take any effective steps to combat the spread of communism right here in Canada. I think we shall face more dangers from internal sources during the next ten or fifteen years than we shall ever face from forces from the outside.
Those who promote the cause of international communism are not fooling this group one bit with their protestations of pious anxiety for the welfare of the ordinary Canadian. Their aim is not to make the lot of the ordinary man any better; their aim is power for themselves. In reality they have the most callous indifference to the sufferings of human beings. The promoters of international communism hold life very cheaply, but they worship the god of power which they hope to have rule over the lives of men and the economies of nations.
However, let us not make any mistake by thinking that they have little or no appeal to the unfortunates, the downtrodden and discontented people of this and every other country in the world. They work with diabolical cleverness and have tremendous influence over the unwary. It is surprising how many people find themselves unwitting tools in the hands of these promoters of international confusion. For example, during the course of the Winnipeg flood propaganda was circulated asking for immediate help for the people of Winnipeg, but right in the middle of that propaganda was this sentence:
Canadian welfare must come first-not preparations for atomic-bacteria warfare.
Now that war has come to some part of the globe things like this are being circulated:
Let Canada act to save world peace. "It is not too late," declares Tim Buck, national leader of the Labour-Progressive party, "to stop this insane rush to disaster." Read this stirring plea by the foremost spokesman of the Canadian working class for unity around proposals that can help save peace.
The Budget-Mr. Thomas
Then this sort of thing from the Stockholm peace conference has come through the mail to all hon. members. It is quite apparent that they are quite willing to put forward any excuse to discredit the capitalist and democratic countries in the world.
Newspaper reports of the past four or five years in Canada indicate that communists have followed a very clever program of infiltration. They have got themselves into home and school groups in an effort to use this medium for the promotion of communist ideology. They have infiltrated into the labour unions and achieved many positions of leadership. I am happy that the Canadian Congress of Labour and the Canadian Federation of Labour have taken action to oust known communists from positions of leadership, but reports in the papers of the past few days indicate that there are still many communists who have managed to get themselves elected as delegates to represent their unions at labour congresses. I suppose one can safely say that infiltration has proceeded into practically every phase of Canadian activity. There is every reason why international communists should concentrate their efforts on the labour unions because Lenin stated at the Russian communist party congress in 1921, when referring to the Russian trade unions:
Not they form the nation; not they are the dictatorship of the proletariat; that is the task of the communist party.
In other words what Lenin was saying was that once the unions had done the wrecking job their usefulness would be finished and any attempt on their part to revive the function of the unions as protesting bodies against bad wages or working conditions would be branded as a capitalist survival and punished by banishment to a slave labour camp. The American Federation of Labor survey of April, 1947, stated that there were then more people permanently hungry and starving in the Russian slave labour camps than were ever temporarily hungry in the worst unemployment in any capitalist land. .
It is therefore essential in their own interests that the labour unions of this country continue to clean house and to banish from the organization every known communist whose purpose is not forthright or whose motives prove to be ulterior in any degree. Time alone can tell whether a communist's association with any one of the labour movements is harmful or detrimental to the broad interests of all members and all groups within the movement. But when time does reveal that a communist and his activities are harmful to the interests of the members of the union,

The Budget-Mr. Thomas then I think that union is obligated to expel him and keep the spotlight on him until he changes his heart.
I have often said that Canada's internal danger from communism is not so much from the registered members of the communist party as it is from those people who allow themselves to become fellow travellers or sympathizers or mere tools in the hands of the communist party. These make up the much more insidious group. It was only last week that we saw a demonstration around this building by a large number of misguided people, among whom it is doubtful if one could find more than a few out and out communists. These people, although not registered members of the communist party, can be just as useful to the cause of communism as are the out and out members.
It has been said over and over again that communism feeds on discontent and thrives among those who are victims of social injustice. I think that is largely true in any country, but it does not account for the attitude of mind of many of those who have become leaders in the communist movement. The real communist is activated by the hope that same day he will be in a position of power over the lives of men. He looks forward to the day when he can crack his whip and force obedience to his orders. For that reason it is not wholly true to say that the correction of injustice within Canada would put an end to the spread of communism.
But these little dictators, these guttersnipes who would sell their country into the hands of the Russian imperialist ring could no longer play their nefarious game with any success among a contented and happy and secure people. That is why it is so important that we make every effort to banish from among the people of Canada all those conditions upon which communism might thrive. That is also why it is imperative that Canada and the other nations of the world make every effort to banish the same conditions in other lands. This must be done if we are to prevent the further spread of this insidious foe of human liberty.
That is why I have felt that this budget is not all that it could have been. As long as thousands of Canadian people are discontented because of the tremendously high cost of living and other social Injustices there will remain fertile ground in which communist activities can grow and spread. As was stated by my leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), I think effective steps could have been taken under this budget to set right those things that are causing the high cost of living. I appeal to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his colleagues 

to take action without further delay to see that the Canadian dollar is stabilized at a level that will return reasonable prices to producers and at the same time make possible reasonable consumer prices. It is not an impossible task by any means. If that is done, if steps are taken to abolish profiteering, and if those of our population who are living on fairly low fixed incomes are given some sort of adjustment, let us say in the nature of a cost of living bonus, I feel certain that the Canadian people will be united in their efforts, not only to resist the spread of communism in Canada but to put an end to aggression wherever it may be on the face of the earth.

In our efforts to manufacture and distribute goods at the lowest price consistent with the increasing standard of living, we have reexamined almost every phase of the production and distribution process. This continuing study has resulted in great and constant change so that the manufacture and movement process today looks quite different from that of fifty years ago. In that period we have progressed from a simple to a highly industrialized and complex society. Some of the most original changes have taken place in the packaging and availability of all types of low-priced goods. A greater variety and quantity of low-priced products are now available to our people than ever before in history. Most reasonably priced goods are sold by the transfer of coins rather than on credit. An undetermined but nevertheless large number of millions of dollars of merchandise and services are thus traded year after year; yet today we still have the same variety of coins in our currency that existed nearly fifty years ago. With all the changes we have made, it would seem logical that we look at the penny, nickel, dime and quarter to determine whether they adequately fit our needs. An analysis of present conditions in buying habits truly reveals the necessity for new coinage to make our system flexible, convenient and economical.
Let me briefly summarize the advantages of two and one-half and seven and one-half cent coins:
1.	The half nickel and nickel and a half coin would provide added flexibility and convenience in making payments at any price level.
2.	Two and one-half and seven and one-half cent coins combine readily with present coins to make pricing possible at present popular five, ten, fifteen and twenty-five cent levels.
3.	The half nickel and nickel and a half represent an orderly and logical sequence of mid-points within our present multiple nickel pricing system, whether used alone or in combination with other coins.
4.	The two and one-half and seven and one-half cent coins provide in effect a one-half cent coin without actually minting such a coin, and take full advantage of the flexibili ty provided by one-half cent pricing.

5.	Two and one-half and seven and one-half cent coins fit into our present coin packaging system. Our present coins are rolled in lots of either forty or fifty to make even dollar amounts. The two and one-half and seven and one-half cent coins could be packaged in lots of forty each to give a roll value of one dollar and three dollars respectively.
6.	Two and one-half cent and seven and one-half cent coins encourage pricing closer to value and permit the one-half cent pricing, such as two for fifteen cents.
7.	The two and one-half and seven and one-half cent coins have been approved by competent economic authorities as economically sound.
8.	Historically the half nickel is a success. The equivalent to two and one-half cent coins has been used successfully for a great many years in Holland, Panama and Ecuador.
Let it be known that I do not contend that this proposal will be the panacea for all the economic evils suffered by the Canadian housewife or wage earner, but I do contend it would be a contributing factor toward a betterment of the situation, and I believe all contributing factors should be considered and, if found desirable, put into action. I realize there will be opposition to this plan by those who are always opposed to any change in the status quo. Opposition, it seems, comes in the form of resistance to change, and the apathy of people in industries most needing this new coinage. Their apathy arises from their belief that it is virtually impossible to bring about the necessary legislation. This is due to their lack of knowledge of the legislative process, and their inability to appreciate the political effectiveness of the individual.
It is my intention at the next session of parliament to request the government to add two and one-half and seven and one-half cent coins to our present currency. At that time I will give the house a more detailed statement and, I hope, ample proof of the necessity of adopting this proposal. In the meantime I would welcome suggestions or criticisms from any faction of our society that would be affected by this proposal.

I have read what the report of the royal commission on prices said about the livestock industry. I proceed with another quotation from that report:
On the other hand, we found a number of industries where competitive forces were limited because of the small number of firms in such fields. For instance, there are only three firms in Canada manufacturing primary fertilizer materials and the very high capital investment required for this industry makes it difficult for new firms to enter this field. Another example occurs in primary textiles, where a few big firms dominate the cotton industry and where the three producers of the three types of synthetic yams manufacture the entire Canadian output.
What happens under circumstances such as are mentioned in the report? When goods are being produced in quantities to more than meet the demand in the market do prices come down? Certainly not. But employees are laid off, production is restricted, prices are maintained. I believe that is only a small part of what the prices commission found. They also found that the manufacturers control prices of the manufactured article through the retailer. Shirts are a good example of this. All shirts sold by manufacturers had to be sold by the retailer at a certain price. He was not free to sell at a lower price if he wished. He was compelled to sell at the manufacturer's price, otherwise he would not get his next supply of shirts.
Let me read a little more from the report of the royal commission on prices:
More significant is the growing tendency toward monopolistic competition through brand names and special advertising, price leadership by a few large firms in an industry and resale price maintenance whereby a manufacturer sets the retail price for his product.
Under such circumstances what opportunity is there to bring down prices when supply is

more than sufficient to meet demand? The same thing is carried through in the proposals connected with housing. The minister said Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would advance less money on a house, and this would mean that for the purchase of the house it would require a larger down payment. Just let us think about that for a moment. At the session of 1949 we thought it would be desirable to lower the down payment, so that the poorer people would be able to buy houses. That was understandable and logical, because the greatest difficulty in our housing situation was to provide ways and means whereby those in the lower income brackets could buy or rent homes.
What do we find now? When the government wants to raise a little extra money and wants to curb inflation, does it begin taxing the man who has sufficient money not only to make a large down payment but perhaps to pay cash for it? No; they begin with the man who has not enough to make a small down payment. They increase the down payment and thus make it not only difficult but impossible for those in the lower income brackets to provide themselves with homes.
If there is anything in what we have been saying, not only in all those weeks but in all those years, about the necessity for defeating communism, then surely that is the wrong way to begin. That is the way to make communists, not the way to eliminate them. I believe I said once before in the house that we should do things it is desirable to do, not for the purpose of destroying communism but because those things are good in themselves.

If we do them only in order to contain communism, then we are going to fail just as surely as the sun will rise tomorrow morning; because what will be done will be too little and too late.

The working people will pay for it in work and sweat; and when they have done that they have done their part, then I say those who have the money should pay the financial cost. There is no other way in which we can meet the difficulties which will confront us in the days that are ahead.
I suggest in all earnestness to the government that if they continue to put the burdens of financing the war and of building our defences on the shoulders of the working people of this country, we may be able to drive the North Koreans back to the 38th parallel but, as surely as we do, we will build communism in this fair land of Canada.

speechtext:
This is not a subject that is new and the view I intend to express is not new. However, I feel called upon to express it because I think it is a valid view and should be expressed in justice to those who are going to be called upon to pay this tax.
The taxes proposed to be increased under this resolution are levied at the manufacturer's level. They are passed on from hand to hand to the wholesaler, to the retailer, to the public, and in some cases also pass through the hands of a jobber.
This tax is subject to two vices. The first is the fact that it is a hidden tax. The consumer is not always conscious, as he ought to be, of paying it and that is one reason why it is popular with governments.
The second vice arises from the fact that it is levied at the manufacturer's level. As the goods are passed on from hand to hand mark-ups are added, which include mark-ups on the tax. That does not yield one cent additional revenue to the country, but it does add greatly to the price the consumer pays. I quite appreciate that there is no tax that does not arouse a certain amount of antagonism. Taxes are never popular. If the Minister of Finance has to find more revenue and is not going to make the necessary economies in order to meet the need, then presumably we are going to have more taxes. While this tax may not hurt a person on low income as much as a direct tax on him nevertheless it does hurt persons with low incomes out of proportion to their incomes.
In the third place, these taxes are consumer taxes. They are based upon consumption. The amount that the poor man pays through these taxes, compared with what the well-to-do man pays, is quite out of proportion to his means. It is obvious that the increases in these taxes are going to be made, but for my part-and I am speaking for myself-I wish to put myself on record, as I have on similar occasions in the past, with regard to taxes of this nature by saying that they are not the kind of taxes that ought to be encouraged by the House of Commons. They are discriminatory against people of small means. They are hidden taxes, and in the third place the consumer pays for more than the tax. The consumer pays the original tax plus the wholesaler's mark-up on 69262-46
Excise Tax Act
the tax, plus the retailer's mark-up on the mark-up on the tax. In that way you will find that in most cases what the consumer pays, by reason of the imposition of the tax, is just about twice as much as the government receives by way of tax levied at the manufacturer's level.

While to those of us who have an electric, gas, wood or coal stove an electric kettle is a luxury, though a very useful one, that is not the case with people living in shared accommodation. If they have young children they probably heat the baby's bottles over an electric element in the bathroom, or use an electric kettle for similar purposes. To these people a kettle is definitely not a luxury; it is just as essential as an electric stove or refrigerator is to a more established family. So 1 suggest that consideration should be given to people living under these conditions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I can state that the government is quite aware of this problem and has made provision for it, because in the classification of electric stoves there are included these various types of hotplates and these new small roasters which are capable of cooking a meal completely. A hotplate is an essential because most of these one or two room apartments to which the hon. member refers are rented by people who cannot afford to have an electric percolator, electric kettle and all the other electrical appliances. They find it simpler to have a hotplate and use an ordinary kettle, and so on. These various types of hotplates and roasters which cook a meal completely are included in the classification of electric stoves.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I am glad to have the parliamentary assistant assure us on this point. Most of these hotplates are one or two burner devices, and I hope the government will give consideration to exempting the electric kettle as being an essential part of the equipment for a small family. These hotplates usually have two burners, and if one is cooking a meal and intends to have a hot beverage one needs another piece of equipment to heat the beverage. I assure the parliamentary assistant that these electric kettles are an essential piece of equipment.
